title: How Ferrari handed Singapore pole to Verstappen
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Ferrari's Formula 1 drivers were rightly disappointed to be on the wrong side of a narrow spread in Singapore Grand Prix qualifying as both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton could have denied Max Verstappen pole.

Just over a tenth of a second separated the trio around the Marina Bay circuit in a Q3 session that had the door left open given Verstappen failed to improve on his final lap - but Leclerc's late leap was not enough, and Hamilton went slower than he had before.

Red Bull finally has a car that Verstappen can hustle to the top spot at the only regular circuit from his F1 career he had not scored a pole or won at prior to this weekend.

But, not to detract from Red Bull's obvious progress, and Verstappen's own quality lap, his description of it being "enough for pole" was exactly right. For he did not have the quickest car in this session and Leclerc, and especially Hamilton, will be lamenting how Q3 played out.

"The car had potential for pole today, but we didn't have a smooth enough session in order to do the job," said Leclerc. "And Max just did a better job."

The Ferrari pair's pole bids failed at different points. For Leclerc, Q3 was a huge salvage job after struggling throughout Q1 and Q2, and the only reason he was in the mix at all was "I just committed a little bit more in Q3 on the last lap".

But it was probably the spectre of braking issues in those sessions that haunted him when it counted, as he conceded it was "taking off quite a lot of confidence".

Bleeding time in the Turn 13 hairpin, where he lost almost a tenth compared to Hamilton with slightly weak rotation, and being too conservative braking for the Turn 16-17 chicane were Leclerc's undoing.

For Turn 16, where Leclerc lost the bulk of his 0.161s deficit to Verstappen in sector three, he just did not attack enough under braking so arrived slightly undercooked - as evidenced by hooking his front right wheel over the inside kerb at a corner you ideally wanted to be just gliding past it along the white line to maximum speed into and through the corner.

But Leclerc was also generally not quite as mighty as Hamilton through the middle sector, where the Ferrari's superiority was unchallenged, so he did not quite gain enough on Verstappen here to offset the weaker final sector. There was perhaps further evidence of his uncertainty under braking: holding a higher gear than Hamilton at a few points around the lap, including leaving it in third for Turns 8 and 14, which Hamilton took in second.

Hamilton has looked a lot more comfortable being so aggressive on corner entry, and was electric through Q1 and Q2. He was much more at one with Ferrari and really extracting the most of its impressive poise under braking and sharp front end into the slower, 90-degree corners especially.

But having been quickest in the first two segments he only managed to go 0.033s quicker in Q3.

"The car felt amazing in Q1 and Q2, and when I finished the laps, I was like, ‘she's got more in her'," he said.

"And the only way in order to try and extract that is to try and add wing. I think it just tipped it over the edge.

"It was only like one hole or something like that. After that the car was just snappy, and none of the laps in Q3 are any good."

Combined they were, though. Hamilton's theoretical best Q3 lap, combining his best sectors, would have been good enough for pole position.

1 Verstappen 1m31.373s2 Leclerc 1m31.427s

Ideal lap - best sectors combined

1 Hamilton 1m31.347s2 Verstappen 1m31.373s

But he was too loose through the opening corners of the first lap and too scrappy in the final sector of the second.

On his first lap, Hamilton shipped 0.271s to Verstappen in sector one. This was by virtue of being slightly wide of the apex into the first corner and then - a legacy of this - having to gather up a small moment through Turn 2 before a much bigger slide followed as he cranked the lock on chucking it into Turn 3.

His middle sector was magnificent, 0.273s quicker than Verstappen. At this point, Hamilton was on for pole - but being ever so slightly hot into Turn 16 just delayed him getting back on the power as he switched back for the second part of the chicane.

On the second run, a tidier first sector and a good but not great middle sector had him in the mix again going into the final part of the lap but an untidy run through 16 and 17 again, with Hamilton sawing at the wheel, meant the lap ended up even slower than the first.

For both drivers, on another day or against a different rival, their small imperfections may not have cost pole. But Verstappen was so strong that he - as he often does - gladly took advantage of others not doing as good a job.

And the Red Bull looked good, too, especially through corners that required a bit more speed on entry. His lap started very purposefully with the front end nice and sharp through the opening sequence of corners and the rear keeping up well. But it was clearly weaker braking and getting the front in for a lot of the 90-degree slower corners in the middle sector, with Verstappen evidently more cautious braking for Turn 7 and then never quite as convincing through the rest of the middle sector.

It came back to him at the end of the lap - and holding third gear to the Ferraris' second into Turn 16 and 17 was perhaps a hint at how both car and driver were just more hooked up there - before ending the lap slightly stronger through the fast final corner too.

"The margins are very close between us throughout the whole of qualifying," said Verstappen.

"So, of course, very happy to be on pole because this is the one that I wanted.

"The car has been pretty strong all weekend. Of course, there are always things that you look into that can be better, but it was enough for pole, so very happy with that."

title: 'I haven't found my top form since the Tour de France' – Remco Evenepoel comes up short at Il Lombardia
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Remco Evenepoel has had a turbulent time since his finishing as runner-up in the Tour de France, winning the Grand Prix de Quebec and European Championship road race, and World Championships time trial but was off his best in the road race.

The pendulum of form swung back the wrong way again in Il Lombardia on Saturday, and left the European Champion eventually settling for fourth place.

Evenepoel came into the race as one of the top favourites but when Paul Seixas lit up the race on the Civiglio climb, it was clear he would not be winning it, as he wasn't even among the few riders who could hold the Frenchman's wheel for a short period of time.

Evenepoel chased as the fourth rider on the road, before settling back into a bigger group, and then leading it across the line in Como.

"Personally, I felt good all day, but there was still some fatigue. In the last hour of the race, I didn't feel at my best anymore. I haven't really found my top form since the Tour, and in races like today, that speaks for itself," Evenepoel told Belgian broadcaster at the finish.

Evenepoel described a "tricky moment" when three rival teams launched dangerous riders up the road on the Madonna del Ghisallo, with World Champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) slipping clear and giving their teams an excuse to sit back in the bunch.

Evenepoel's Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe teammates managed the situation well and stitched the race back together, but when the race exploded on that crucial section of the Civiglio, Evenepoel's race imploded.

"My legs started to feel heavy on the long climb [Madonna del Ghisallo]. It certainly wasn't my best day on the bike, but it wasn't a bad one either. We have nothing to reproach ourselves for. There were simply stronger riders today," Evenepoel said.

It was an uneventful end to a season that began with a trio of wins in Mallorca in January, the overall Volta a Valenciana in February, a win in the Amstel Gold Race and podiums in the Tour of Flanders and Liège-Bastogne-Liège in April before a 69-day break from competition before the best Tour de France performance of his career.

Although his shape has been uneven since the Tour, he still scored his fourth win in the San Sebastian Classic, and even on a bad day in Lombardia, he was still just one rung off the podium.

"Look, it has been quite a long season. Since June, things have been a bit up and down for me, both in training and in races. I've had very good days, but also some weaker ones. And you can see that today. You have to be 100% here, but I wasn't," Evenepoel concluded.

title: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo
author: Nadeem Badshah
text:
Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger

A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire , police have said.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated shortly after the incident and the site will remain closed on Sunday.

South Yorkshire police said that at 1.35pm it received reports of an individual entering the enclosure at the zoo near Doncaster .

The force said the attack “resulted in serious injury”.

The statement added: “Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time.

“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”

The force earlier said: “We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this distressing footage.”

Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.

It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.

“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show a man wearing a black jumper sitting on the ground of the enclosure and being attacked by a tiger.

A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.

title: Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt
author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
text:
Pike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical care

Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee ’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.

Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”

Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.

But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.

Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.

There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.

Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.

Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.

Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.

After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”

Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.

Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation . And the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year, but they continue elsewhere.

For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.

title: Trent Grisham and the Yankees’ flawed philosophy
author: Kento Mizuno
text:
Batting order alone doesn’t dictate a team’s fortune, but it does make a difference. This is especially so in short series, where even the tiniest edges and flaws are magnified. And no place in the lineup matters more than the top spot. Suffice it to say that Aaron Boone and the Yankees faced an extremely important decision when choosing the leadoff man for Game 3 with the season on the line.

So why in the world did they land on Trent Grisham?

To state the obvious, Grisham did not have a good year in any shape or form. He had a .308 OBP. His wRC+ was 98. And these numbers are what he recorded landing on the IL at the start of September with a strained hammy. To his credit, Grisham did record two hits during the party against the dregs of the Red Sox bullpen in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, but he was a non-factor in Games 1 and 2 of the Division Series. This isn’t the resume of someone to whom you’d like to entrust the leadoff spot in an elimination game . And yet, that’s precisely what the Yankees did.

Of course, it’s easy as an armchair manager to fall into the trap of hindsight. It would be wrong of me to point to Grisham’s 0-for-5, three-strikeout night and say, “I told you so.” But that’s not what I’m going to argue. My point is that hitting Grisham first was the wrong call, even if it had worked out, because the decision-making process had a fatal flaw — one that explains so much about this current era of Yankees baseball.

That flaw is this: the Yankees’ way of evaluating players has become far too rigid. Once they make up their mind about a player’s true talent, they will adhere to it adamantly, even if the on-field results suggest that something is wrong. It takes a mountain of evidence to pile up for them to consider recalibrating their view of that player, and by the time that happens, the damage has already been done.

Trent Grisham is but the latest example. When asked postgame whether he regretted placing Grisham in the leadoff spot, Aaron Boone had this to offer:

“ No. I mean, look, obviously, we really struggled to score runs in the first two games, and I was pretty convicted on trying to find a way to be able to get Benny a chance to come up with runners on or be in a position to do that more often tonight…it’s a decision I made to try and create a little bit of traffic, and obviously it didn’t work. But you’re going to live with that.”

I get wanting to give Ben Rice more chances to hit with men on base. But even if that made sense, Grisham was not the answer. The man isn’t a high-OBP guy. Not counting 2020, his career high over a full season is the .348 mark he posted last year; in all other years he’s failed to reach .330. He’s a high-walk guy, I’ll give him that, but his abysmal batting averages have generally dragged his OBP down to unremarkable levels. To wit: Grisham’s career walk rate is a robust 12.1 percent, but his career OBP is a pedestrian .319.

Boone’s reasoning only makes sense if you assume that Grisham’s superb 2025 represented a new baseline for him, and that version of him was still somewhere within him, despite his subpar 2026 numbers and his late-season injury. It seems, in short, that Boone and the Yankees were clinging to the best version of Grisham in their minds, a version detached from reality.

When viewed in this way, the Grisham decision turns from an isolated blunder to the latest case of a widespread issue. Recall how the Yankees kept running Austin Wells out until June, despite him hitting for a 26 wRC+ for the entire month of May. The team only took action when Wells went to them , suggesting that they might have been unaware that something was ailing Wells if he hadn’t.

I don’t think it’s too farfetched to theorize that they viewed Wells’ disastrous offensive performance as merely a bad slump, and that they were planning on simply running him out there until he experienced positive regression, without making any inquiries into his health. The Yankees had an idea of how Austin Wells was supposed to hit, and when the on-field results weren’t there, they assumed that their idea of Wells would eventually translate to reality, rather than readjusting their evaluation of Wells given recent results.

Wells’ case is reminiscent of how the Yankees handled Anthony Rizzo’s concussion in 2023. It took 46 games of Rizzo hitting .172/.271/.225 for the Yankees to do anything, and even then, Rizzo had to go to the team , not the other way around. And this goes beyond how the Yankees have mismanaged injuries; in 2024, we saw them keep trotting out Alex Verdugo in left field when it was clear by mid-July that it wasn’t working out. In 2025, they stubbornly kept on using Devin Williams in high-leverage situations, a crucial factor in them losing the division race. Then there’s the ongoing shortstop question, with the Yankees being stubborn at various points about both Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Anthony Volpe’s abilities. Time and time again, the Yankees of recent years have shown a reluctance to change their minds about their own players.

Admittedly, there is something to be said for not overreacting to small sample sizes. Even superstars can have bad weeks and months; look at how Pete Crow-Armstrong and Fernando Tatis Jr. started their respective years, compared to the numbers they finished with. Closer to home in 2024, Aaron Judge followed an awful April with a preposterous .352/.488/.777 triple slash with 52 homers in 127 games as he won MVP. Making rash, drastic changes based on the tiniest fluctuations in performance is not a winning formula by any means.

However, there needs to be a balance. Teams can, and should, try to constantly update their understanding of players’ abilities based on new data, while keeping in mind that small sample size caveats apply. Right now, the Yankees’ modus operandi appears as though it’s set in stone. If that’s due to a philosophical stance about trying not to be influenced by granular data points, then that stance needs to be relaxed. And if that’s due to complacency and hubris, then I’d like to remind them that it’s been 17 years since their last title. Something needs to change.

title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
author: Sammy Gecsoyler
text:
Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful

Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel .

The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.

The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, having Palestine Action placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests.

Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.

Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march.

The Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.

The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.

“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”

The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.

At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches , which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”

Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”

Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.

“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.

The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.

A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.

The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.

Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.

The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.

The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.

title: Winners and losers from Singapore GP 2026 F1 qualifying
author: Josh Suttill
text:
A better evening for the championship leader’s upgraded car still wasn’t enough to get Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes into the Singapore Grand Prix pole fight , so it’s turning into a very good weekend for (one) Red Bull.

Here’s our full winners and losers rundown from qualifying.

Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)

Max Verstappen might just be one good start away from finally ending his Singapore hex and taking a grand prix victory on the one remaining circuit he has raced at regularly in F1 without winning.

He’s looked hooked up in the Red Bull this weekend as the 2026 car looks much more suited to the Marina Bay street circuit than its ground-effect predecessors ever did.

It wasn’t perfect. That Verstappen couldn’t improve on his final run left him vulnerable. But there’s no better place to start from if Verstappen is to make it two wins on the spin: although he’s clearly still not convinced by Red Bull’s startline troubles.

He was mugged off the line by George Russell in the sprint and Verstappen says there are “no excuses” for this given the sister Racing Bulls team is having good launches with the same software and hardware.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (22nd)

A session that left the other Red Bull driver “pissed off” and wishing he’d stayed at home.

Isack Hadjar commended the work done by his Red Bull mechanics to get him out on track before a gearbox issue that “broke the fourth gear” and caused another abrupt end.

Hadjar was less than pleased after qualifying ended and went into somewhat of a spiral in his media session about his dislike for the current sprint format, the future sprint races and the “very disappointing” decision-making that led to more sprints being put on the calendar.

Part of the Red Bull driver’s frustration comes from having his excitement of getting over his handling issues ruined and the chance of points on Sunday now looking far from reality. Or, as he rather amusingly summed up: “I could’ve stayed back in Paris and it would’ve been the same [result.]”

Winner: Upgraded Mercedes (4th)

Kimi Antonelli’s gap to pole was cut from seven tenths to two tenths of a second from Friday to Saturday, a victory for the upgraded Mercedes.

Antonelli said: “We went completely opposite with the set-up [after the sprint race], and the car was in a happier place”.

The Race understands that the balance shift took the car away from generating too much oversteer and giving Antonelli a lack of confidence under braking.

Antonelli played around with differential settings during the sprint that dialled a lot of that oversteer out - leading to stronger pace later in the race - and that was followed by major set-up changes after the sprint, including raising the ride height and thus moving the aero balance back into a better window.

He thinks Mercedes should switch both its drivers to the new package for the next race at Austin so the team can keep experimenting to find the right window for its new upgrade.

Russell, a largely meaningless sixth in qualifying with a hefty engine penalty to serve for the race, wasn’t quite as glowing.

“It was positive to see Kimi more competitive today than yesterday, however, we weren't exactly lighting the timing screen on fire,” Russell said.

“As a team we’re still not satisfied with where we are with the new package. We recognise we need to make set-up adjustments to compensate for those changes. Maybe we can find a way to make it work, but right now we need more time.”

The upgraded Mercedes is still lagging behind the Red Bull and the Ferrari in Singapore at least, but it’s clearly made a step in the right direction.

Loser: Aston Martin (17th + 19th)

A messy session that may leave Aston Martin even worse off than the initial qualifying results suggest.

Fernando Alonso already suggested he may take a grid penalty for a turbo issue that progressively worsened throughout Saturday’s action, culminating in a loss of power and momentum on the exits of the corners and a Q1 exit.

A lockup and a little bit of traffic were the story on the other side of the garage, as Lance Stroll surmised that the main Aston Martin issue comes from the bumpy nature of the Marina Bay circuit not working for its current package.

Given the track conditions are unlikely to change overnight, and the low grid positions could get even lower, the reality is a far cry from the pre-event aspirations of another potential points haul.

Winner: Charles Leclerc (2nd)

After a bruising sprint where he faded badly with front tyre wear, this was Charles Leclerc at his best - dancing through discomfort to pull a very good qualifying lap out from nowhere.

He lagged badly behind Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton in Q1 and Q2, struggling with the car pulling to one side under braking, but with more “commitment” he turned the tables in Q3 and even got surprisingly close to pole.

Leclerc suggested he still wasn’t entirely happy with the car so, even beyond a front-row start typically being a good qualifying result, this worked out very well.

Loser: Lewis Hamilton (3rd)

Context is critical for establishing why Hamilton ultimately lost out in qualifying.

Third on the grid is fine, especially when the gaps were so small. But it could have been so much more.

Leclerc said there was more in the Ferrari and Hamilton was the evidence. His theoretical best lap in Q3 was quicker than Verstappen’s, so if he had pieced together the sectors, he would be first. Plain and simple.

Hamilton had been delighted with his runs through Q1 and Q2 so to have that final outcome, after a Q3 in which he said neither lap was any good, is a loss. -

Loser: Franco Colapinto (16th)

Eight places down on Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly was more like the Franco Colapinto of old, rather than the driver who has been on terms with Gasly for much of the second half of the season.

Colapinto ended up in the wall in Q2 at Turn 17 but even before then he wasn’t looking likely to join Gasly in Q3.

“It's very strange,” Colapinto said of his 16th place. “Before the wall, I was already a lot slower than my Q1 lap, which normally you would improve a lot.

“So, I don't know, very strange, I had no rear grip the last lap. It was extremely poor, it was the worst balance I've had in the weekend.

“So, I don't know, a bit lost, to be honest, because Q1 felt quite easy to do the lap and it was coming not too bad, but then it was very, very poor.”

Winner: Pierre Gasly (8th)

For the third consecutive grand prix qualifying session, Gasly won F1’s midfield battle, beating both Racing Bulls in Q3.

Gasly called it “one of my best Q3s of the year” in a season he took pole at Monza, as he was thrilled with his execution on a sprint weekend.

He’s just hoping his Q3 appearance will translate into points, unlike in Azerbaijan and Malaysia.

“I must say the last few weekends, I think we have done four Q3s [including Singapore sprint] in the last four quali, but somehow we haven't scored that much because it's always gone wrong for whatever reason,” Gasly said.

“So as much as I would like a bit of chaos tomorrow, [it’s] hopefully not involving us another time, and hopefully we can translate this good quali into points.”

Alex Albon was half a second slower than Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz in Q1 despite being “relatively happy with my lap”.

The data suggests the majority of that loss seems to come with the way Albon approached the tricky Turn 13 left-hander.

Team boss James Vowles said Albon “wasn’t as comfortable in the car” after Williams made repairs following the sprint, in which he shunted into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto’s Audi at the safety car restart.

Sainz’s Q2 was also compromised as Williams’s systems indicated he’d taken the chequered flag when he actually hadn’t - so he abandoned his lap and with it any chance of beating the Haas drivers.

“We will have a look overnight and see what changes we need to do so both drivers can come back stronger tomorrow,” Vowles said. -

title: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
author: Terrence O’Brien
text:
A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.

A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.

Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained , and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger has confirmed that “one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.”

Photos and videos posted on X and Threads appear to show a small circuit board sandwiched under the screen. The implant allegedly intercepts anything displayed on the screen, including the seed passphrase shown during the initial setup. Using an embedded SIM card, the implant then sends that information back to the attacker, who can then siphon funds from user accounts.

Reports indicate that whoever is behind the hack has stolen over $86 million worth of crypto from hundreds of wallets. There’s no indication that Ledger’s systems have been compromised or that wallets purchased directly from the company have been affected. Instead, the issue appears to be a supply chain attack primarily involving users in Southeast Asia and the CryptoBillis reseller. Ledger has provided guidance on how to check if your wallet has been tampered with.

title: 'I just went into the red and that was it' – Tom Pidcock pays for following Paul Seixas' race-winning move in Il Lombardia
author: Matilda Price
text:
Pinarello-Q36.5's Tom Pidcock was briefly one of the only riders who could stick with winner Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) during his race-winning attack in Il Lombardia , but ultimately paid for his effort and finished off the podium.

Pidcock and his team – who can't currently match the horsepower of the peloton's biggest squads – raced a smart race, keeping the Brit near the front without exerting themselves too much, and he was in a good place going into the finale.

When Seixas cranked up the pace on the Civiglio climb, big favourites like Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) and Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) were immediately dropped, but Pidcock, along with Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek), was able to hang onto his wheel, albeit briefly.

"I had a bad position going into the penultimate climb, I made a bit of an effort to come to the front and then went a little bit deep on the wheel of Paul and paid for it," Pidcock explained at the finish.

"But I felt really good today, just that climb, I just went into the red, and that was it. But it was OK."

Asked about Seixas' race-winning effort, Pidcock accepted that there wasn't much he or anyone could have done to match his acceleration on the climb, which the Frenchman explained was earlier than planned because "the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb – for me at least – to make the difference".

"He didn't really attack, he just kind of made his own pace, a high pace," Pidcock said. "He was super strong."

Pidcock was initially the first chaser, but was passed by the likes of Enric Mas (Movistar) and Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) who would eventually fill out the podium spots. The 27-year-old found himself in the main chasing group with Evenepoel, Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and others, eventually taking sixth on the line.

Though Pidcock has had a string of top results this autumn – including two runner-up spots in the Italian Classics – the fact he missed out on another big result on Saturday was not a major source of disappointment.

"Good," was his summary of the late-season campaign. "Today I think I also suffered from not knowing the route so well, it was the first time I'd done it this way, so definitely I think that's an advantage. But no excuses, wasn't strong enough, and so it is."

He still has a few more shots at success before the year is out, though, as he will now head to the Tour of Guangxi t o finish his season in China.

title: 'It hasn't been the easiest year' - Marianne Vos finishes a tough season on a history-making high at the UCI Gravel World Championships
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
The Dutch rider had earmarked the race and was excited about it long before it was on most people's radar, as she had a history in Nannup, having come to the Margaret River Tour several times in the last decade. Now she has also made history there, with the world title she claimed in the small town in the south of Western Australia, her 15th across several disciplines and her second in gravel. That makes her the first rider ever to double up at Gravel Worlds, which is in its fifth edition.

Vos , who lost her father earlier this year, had understandably come into the event relatively low on season race days. In her last gravel race before Saturday, she was dropped by the German 2024 Unbound winner, Rosa Klöser. Vos was determined not to let the same thing happen again when the pair led in the last section of the race.

Vos and Klöser got away after the lead group caught an attacking Tiffany Cromwell (Australia) on the Folly climb with around 25km to go. When Klöser attacked, the only rider she couldn't budge was Vos, who had also been steadfast at the front throughout the 125.6km race with 3179m of elevation gain.

"I knew I had a chance when I was able to follow, but also the downhill was a tricky one, the last one," Vos told the media after the win as she referred to the final descent to the line. "I wanted to go in front and unfortunately Rosa crashed, so then I didn't know what advantage I had.

"I tried to push until the finish, and then of course I was very happy to be crossing the line first."

Even with the long list of world titles to her name, it was clear that this one meant a lot as she celebrated while crossing the line. After a mud-spattered hug for her girlfriend, she was quick to go to her rival Klöser with a sympathetic embrace for the rider who was wearing the marks of her crash, which came with just under 4km to go and left her with bloody wounds on her thigh and arm.

"I was sad that she crashed because that's not a nice way to beat the competition, but unfortunately that happened," said Vos. The German rider came down as she took an inside line while trying to come to terms with Vos after she had forced the pace to get to the front for the final downhill run to the line.

As Vos crossed the finish line, the cheers from those on the sidelines were undoubtedly enthusiastic, with a Vos victory probably only second on the wish list for the local crowd to an Australian one. It was also something of a mutual appreciation society.

"It was a fantastic course here in Australia," said Vos in a statement from her Visma-Lease a Bike team. "I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here."

It's an outcome she was far from certain of when she committed to the target, but that perhaps makes it even more special.

"It hasn't been the easiest year, and actually coming here I didn't really know what to expect. I also wasn't my best over the last month, so I tried to do everything I could to get ready and get in the best possible shape to be ready for the start.

"And, yeah, I think that all worked out pretty well," said Vos, who is now heading into her end-of-season break with a new rainbow jersey in her luggage.

title: Dozens reported injured in Yemeni Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor and agencies
text:
Saudi authorities yet to confirm strike as government-allied forces in Yemen claim successful offensive to retake Bab al-Mandab strait

Yemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport in Saudi Arabia , with dozens reported wounded and a witness describing panic in the terminal.

Donald Trump told reporters he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen .

“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.

“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told Agence France-Presse. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”

A source at a local hospital told the news agency that five people were in intensive care after being wounded at the airport, and “dozens” more had been injured.

The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.

Witnesses said people were being evacuated from the airport.

Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.

The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.

A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.

“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”

By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”

The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.

An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.

It is thought that as many as 500 Houthis fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.

The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – the poorest country in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.

The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.

There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

title: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania
author: Marina Dunbar
text:
Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat

Nine people, including children, died in a mass murder on Friday in Erie, Pennsylvania , after a gun-wielding attacker opened fire outside a home and then entered the property, according to authorities.

The suspected attacker was also found dead as police responded to the deadly violence, which triggered a standoff involving Erie police officers and tactical teams.

Police discovered the killings at about 5pm when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities that they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside.

Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered fatal gunshot wounds.

The situation quickly developed into a standoff as police officers and tactical personnel surrounded the residence. More gunshots were heard coming from inside the home, and officers entered the place.

Inside, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding seven additional victims, including children, along with the suspected attacker. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, spoke about the scale of the mass murder, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed.

“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public.”

He added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”

Authorities on Saturday said they were still investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings, with authorities attempting to determine a motive for the violence.

The city of Erie also issued a statement on social media confirming that the suspected shooter had died and that the immediate danger had passed.

The statement described the case as a “terrible tragedy”, although the city’s statement did not provide further information about the events leading up to the shooting.

“We understand that the news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained,” the city said.

Figures from the Gun Violence Archive indicate that the killings in Erie marked at least the 19th mass murder of the year. Such cases are defined as ones in which four or more victims are murdered.

Many of those mass murders have been what are considered family annihilations , in which an attacker kills multiple close family members.

The nonpartisan archive also indicated that the killings in Erie were among more than 500 mass shootings across the US since the beginning of January. Mass shootings are defined as cases in which four or more victims are shot whether fatally or non-fatally.

Mass shootings for years have remained a persistent problem in the US, often intensifying public demands for stronger gun control measures at the federal level.

Despite those calls, Congress has not enacted such restrictions sought over the years.

title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: David Bednar
author: John Griffin
text:
A generation of Yankees fans have been spoiled. First, it was Mariano Rivera — when “Enter Sandman” began to echo through the halls of Yankee Stadium, the game was effectively over. David Robertson “the Houdini” and Andrew Miller “the Game Enderer” locked down the ninth inning so effectively in their one-year stints as the closer that nobody really noticed a difference. Aroldis Chapman exasperated fans, for, well, a lot of reasons, but he’s got a Hall of Fame resume for a reason, and there’s a non-zero chance he ends up there with a Yankee cap. Clay Holmes spent the better part of three seasons as the Yankee closer, making two All-Star appearances, and in his brief stint in the job in 2024, Luke Weaver was a big reason they made the World Series.

In truth, only one closer in the last 30 years has been an unmitigated disaster, and his performance prompted the Yankees to make a swing for his replacement — today’s birthday boy, David Bednar.

David Jeffrey Bednar Born: October 10, 1994 (Pittsburgh, PA) Yankees Tenure: 2025-present

Born in Pittsburgh and raised in the extremely small town of Mars (the Pennsylvania borough, a part of the greater Pittsburgh metropolitan area, has fewer than 1,500 inhabitants), Bednar played baseball for his local high school but — perhaps unsurprisingly, given the size of the school — went undrafted. From there, he went to Lafayette College in Easton, PA, and was en route to Massachusetts after his junior year to play in the Cape Cod Summer League. He never made it there, however, as the San Diego Padres instead made him the 1,044th pick of the 2016 MLB Draft — a pick that, since Rob Manfred shrunk the draft to 20 rounds, no longer exists.

According to the school newspaper, he was just the fourth player ever drafted out of Lafayette, and when he made his MLB debut as a 40-man roster call-up in 2019, he became just the second Lafayette alumnus to make The Show. Between that month and the abbreviated 2020 campaign, Bednar struggled in limited time with the Padres, allowing 13 runs in 17.1 innings across the two years. As such, the Padres had no problem including him as part of the seven-player deal that brought Joe Musgrove to Southern California.

Now with his hometown Pirates, Bednar spent the entire 2021 season in the Majors, and he established himself as one of the league’s most reliable relievers. He posted a 2.23 ERA in 61 games, striking out 77 en route to a down-ballot Rookie of the Year vote. He then took over the closer’s job on a permanent basis the following year, compiling 58 saves and a pair of All-Star nods across the 2022 and 2023 campaigns.

An awful start to 2024, however — he allowed 14 runs in 10 innings in April — prompted the Pirates to remove him from the closer’s role after a disastrous August (10.97 ERA), and when he struggled out of the gate in 2025, they wasted no time and optioned him to Triple-A in the first week of the season.

When he returned to the Majors in late April, though, Bednar recaptured his All-Star self. From April 19th through July 28th, he allowed just seven runs and struck out 50 batters in 37 innings. It was on the back of this dominant performance that the Yankees, eager to rebuild their bullpen, made Bednar a priority at the trade deadline, sending a package centered on catcher Rafael Flores to the Pirates to bring “Renegade” to the Bronx.

Bednar’s introduction to the Yankees was, like that of every player the Yankees acquired at the 2025 deadline, a disaster: called on to bail out fellow acquisition Jake Bird, he allowed two runs on four hits (including one home run) to hand the lead to the Miami Marlins. Fortunately, his second inning of work in that game, in which he struck out two while retiring the side in order, would be much more emblematic of the rest of his 2025 — he allowed just four runs in 23 innings across the final two months of the season, as he brought stability to a closer role that had seen Devin Williams and Luke Weaver struggle. He remained his dominant self that October, allowing a grand total of three hits across six innings, earning the final out in each of the two Wild Card wins as the 2025 Yankees became the first team since the new playoff format was introduced to advance to the ALDS after dropping Game 1 of the Wild Card.

Bednar began 2026 by joining Team USA for this year’s World Baseball Classic, and while the United States squad embarrassed itself in pool play against Italy and ultimately lost in the championship to Venezuela, none of that was his fault: he provided four scoreless innings in middle relief as part of a stacked bullpen, allowing just six baserunners and striking out eight. Unfortunately, following the tournament, he got off to a shaky start to the season, culminating in a disastrous blown save against the Mets on May 17th in which he allowed three runs.

After that day, though, Bednar became lights-out, surrendering just 11 runs (eight earned) in his final 44 appearances of the season, with just two blown saves in that stretch. While his early slow struggles kept him from making his third career All-Star appearance, he ended the season tied for fifth in saves (35) and 14th among relievers in fWAR (1.9). Sure, he needed his emotional support baserunners far too often for my liking, but at the end of the day, few relievers were as reliable as he was in 2026.

At the end of this season, Bednar hits free agency, and at this point, it’s not clear whether the Yankees will look to retain their closer — after all, they haven’t really signed a reliever to a big long-term deal in half a decade, and on top of that, Bednar is on the wrong side of 30. (That’s a discussion for another day.) Whether he stays or goes, though, he was one of the bright spots in the Yankee bullpen over the last two seasons.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here .

title: Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore pole
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen took his second pole position in a week by beating the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix.

Verstappen's first lap in final qualifying was enough to take pole, his time fending off a second lap from Leclerc that was 0.054 seconds off pole.

Hamilton was closest to Verstappen after the first runs but was unable to improve on his second run.

In fact, most of the front runners struggled to improve on their second runs, as Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli took fourth on the grid, from McLaren's Lando Norris.

Antonelli's team-mate George Russell was sixth fastest but will drop to the back of the grid with a penalty for using too many engine parts.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was the only driver in the top four teams other than Leclerc to improve on his second run but could do no better than qualify seventh.

Alpine's Pierre Gasly and the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out

Verstappen came to Singapore fresh from his and Red Bull's first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and he has continued where he left off.

The four-time champion has looked the man to beat all weekend, and took pole for the grand prix a few hours after winning the sprint, following Russell crashing out of the lead.

Verstappen said: "This was the one I really wanted. The car has been really strong all weekend.

"We have been on a really on a positive trend and it's really special to take the pole here."

Leclerc felt pole had been on the cards if he had not made a few small mistakes on his final lap.

He said: "Q1 and Q2 were really difficult. I had some weird struggles under braking. Q3, the lap was OK. I did some mistakes. I think there was a potential to be on pole today but Max just did a better job."

Hamilton, second to Verstappen in the sprint, was quickest in the first and second parts of qualifying but could not repeat that pace when it mattered during what he described as "another difficult Q3".

He added: "The car was feeling much better. I really felt she had more in her, pushing her through the laps and sessions. Q1 and Q2 were awesome, but got to Q3, snaps through (Turns) One and Three (on the first lap) put me down and rest of the lap was good, and then the second lap too many snaps.

"I think there's a really fine line with our car whether you are over or under the sweet spot and I didn't get it quite right today."

title: Sublime Seixas Becomes Youngest-Ever Winner of IL Lombardia with Huge Solo Move
author: sstokes
text:
Paul Seixas wins Il Lombardia (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Paul Seixas further underlined his staggering talent with an assured win at Il Lombardia , taking the first Monument win of his career and becoming the youngest-ever winner.

The 20 year old drove forward with 19.2km to go to drop most of the other big contenders on the Civiglio, the penultimate climb of the day. He went over the top well clear of European championships runner-up Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), with the latter being replaced by Vuelta winner Enric Mas (Movistar)

Seixas powered up the second and final ascent of the San Fermo Della Battaglia, with Mas dropping Ciccone in a bid to close up to him.

However he was far too strong, racing in well clear and savoring the biggest win of his career.

Mas raced in for second place, 48 seconds back, with Ciccone taking third in his final race for his team.

Seixas looked stunned by what he had done, and said that things hadn’t really sunk in by the time he did the post-race interview.

“It is crazy. I think I don’t realize [it] for now,” he said. “Everything went perfect, the team did a great, awesome job. Everyone pushed more than what they had to do.”

His Decathlon CMA CGM team did indeed dedicate themselves to him, helping him to save energy until it most counted.

“I had amazing legs. I had the feeling that today was a great day,” he continued. “I managed to make the difference at the moment I choose. Maybe a bit earlier because I felt like the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb, for me at least, to make the difference.

“So I had to accelerate early, maybe a bit too early. There were some not really steep parts, so I had to manage really well my effort and accelerate in the hard parts. I did the best TT I could, me against myself. It was crazy.”

New European champion Remco Evenepoel had to be satisfied with fourth place, something well below his pre-race ambitions. He crashed in Il Lombardia in his 2020 debut, going over the side of a bridge and falling several meters to the ground.

He fractured his pelvis and has tried to win the race several time since. He was second to Tadej Pogačar in 2024 and 2025 and with Pogačar absent due to injury, he felt he might have his big victory this time around.

That optimism was furthered by his victory in the Euros last weekend but, once the pressure was applied, he found himself slipping backwards and losing contact with the other big challengers.

Just as was the case at the worlds, he dangled off the back of the groups his rival were in, but eventually fought his way forward again towards the end. He led the sprint in for fourth place, 1:20 back, with new world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG) continuing his stomping end of season with fifth place.

“I think I had bad position going into the penultimate climb,” he said. “I made a bit of an effort to come to the front and went a little deep on the wheel of Paul and paid for it.

“I felt really good today. But then that climb, I went into the red. That was it.”

The final Monument of the season was, as ever, a very tough one. It packed in 4662 vertical meters over 239km, and was enlivened by a big breakaway sparked off 211 kilometers out by Uno-X Mobility rider Johannes Kulse.

Andrea Mifsud (Team Polti VisitMalta), Micahel Leonard, Ben O’Connor (Jayco-AlUla) and Maxime Decomble (Groupama-FDJ United) got across, while Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain Victorious), Sylvain Moniquet (Cofidis), Fausto Masnada (MBH Bank Csb Telecom Fort), George Bennett, Pau Martí (NSN), Gijs Leemreize (Picnic PostNL) and Louis Vervaeke (Soudal Quick-Step) did likewise soon afterwards.

Julien Bernard (Lidl-Trek) and Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) made it 14 and together they build a lead of almost three minutes.

O’Connor hacked down the break’s size when he set a furious pace on the Ghisallo. Their lead was 1:29 with 61.5km remaining, with the pace heating up behind when Louis Barre (Visma-Lease a Bike) went all out to platform a huge move by Matteo Jorgenson.

The American was joined by compatriots Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) and Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG), as well as the Italian Christian Scaroni (XDS Astana).

However Giulio Pellizzari put in a huge effort and brought them back several kilometers later, then continued to plough along at the front for Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe. Simmons had been the fastest up the Ghisallo but had the misfortune to experience a mechanical, ruining his chances.

Pellizzari continued to set a determined pace on the climb of San Fermo Della Battaglia and put Jorgenson, Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Juan Ayuso (Lidl-Trek) and Lenny Martinez (Bahrain-Victorious) out the back. His efforts ensured the break had just 44 seconds crossing the finish line with 21.8km to go, and while Leonard pushed clear alone soon afterwards on the climb of Civiglio, he was reeled in soon afterwards.

Isaac Del Toro was the big hope for UAE and Adam Yates did most of the work on that climb. However it was Seixas who was strongest. He stomped away with 19.2km remaining, Pidcock and Ciccone clinging on briefly before being forced to slow.

Pidcock’s place in the chase was taken by soon afterwards by Mas, with the Vuelta winner dropping Ciccone on the San Fermo Della Battaglia but having zero success in trying to get back up to Seixas.

The Frenchman was absolutely flying. He may have been the youngest rider in the whole race but he was far above the level of the rest.

“It is a dream. Today my legs made me dream today and then I had an opportunity,” he smiled.

“I really trained hard for this. It is incredible.”

It is, and it set things up for some fascinating clashes with Pogačar next season.

Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Procycling) was sixth, with nine riders in total in this group.

title: Trump Turns to Russia as Diesel Prices Rise
text: Bloomberg Congressional Reporter Caitlin Reilly and ABC News State Department Reporter Shannon Kingston join hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss President Donald Trump's agreement to obtain Russian diesel as rising energy costs put pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. title: Il Lombardia: Paul Seixas puts in stunning solo ride to claim first Monument
author: Matilda Price
text:
French prodigy Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) became the youngest winner in Il Lombardia history on Sunday, going solo 18km from the line to take a stunning win and cap an outstanding season.

The 20-year-old had his team working on the front all day, but Seixas himself stayed patient until the crucial moment, putting in one big acceleration on the Civiglio climb that no one could follow for more than a minute or two. From there, despite being chased by some of the strongest riders in the world, the Frenchman could not be reeled back in.

Vuelta a España winner Enric Mas (Movistar) ditched the uncooperative Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) in the finale to try and chase down Seixas solo, but his efforts were futile as the Frenchman soloed to victory by 49 seconds.

Mas settled for second, as Ciccone rolled in a few seconds behind him to cap off his career with Lidl-Trek with a third place.

Pre-race favourite Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) sprinted to fourth from the chase group as an unsatisfactory consolation prize, after being visible and active all day but ultimately not being able to react to the crucial move.

Earlier in the day, a 14-man breakaway was up the road for most of the day, with seven riders surviving into the final 20km, but Seixas' move spelled the end of their day, with Michael Leonard (EF Education-EasyPost) the final rider to be caught.

With his win just two weeks after his 20th birthday, Seixas becomes the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia, and the fourth youngest men's Monument victor in history.

"It's crazy. I think I don't realise for now," he said at the finish. "Everything went perfect. The teammates [did a] great, awesome job. Everyone pushed more than what they had to do, and yeah, I had amazing legs.

"I had the feeling that today was a great day, and I managed to make the difference at the moment I chose, maybe a bit earlier, because I felt like the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb – for me at least – to make the difference, so I had to accelerate early, maybe a bit too early. There was some not really steep parts, so I had to manage really efforts and accelerate in the hard parts.

"Then I did the best I could, a TT, me against myself and yeah, it was crazy."

He knew he had a decent gap, but said it was "not enough to think about the win before the end of the last climb".

"Then at the end of the last climb I started believing and I just had to not make mistakes on the downhill, so I was careful. I don't realise [what I've done], I think."

After the 239km race eventually got underway after the peloton staged a protest about safety by delaying the start , business as usual resumed with the attacks starting straight out of the neutral zone. Martin Marcellusi (Bardiani CSF 7 Saber) was the very first rider to attack, but the day's break wasn't going to get away that easily, and the battle continued all the way up the opening climbs.

An initial group of five got away midway up the Selvino climb, but the fight was continuing behind them with multiple counter-attacks, and the leaders were joined over the top of the ascent to make it a 14-rider break.

The riders were: Ben O'Connor (Jayco AlUla), Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain-Victorious), Michael Leonard (EF Education-EasyPost), Maxime Decomble (Groupama-FDJ United), Johannes Kulset (Uno-X Mobility), Andrea Mifsud (Polti VisitMalta), George Bennett, Pau Marti (NSN), Fausto Masnada (MBH Bank CSB Telecom Fort), Gijs Leemreize (Picnic PostNL), Sylvain Moniquet (Cofidis), Louis Vervaeke (Soudal-QuickStep), Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Julien Bernard (Lidl-Trek).

With most big teams represented, the peloton seemed relatively happy to let this break go, and they soon built a gap of two minutes – though they weren't given much more than that as UAE, Red Bull and Decathlon controlled the gap.

Back in the peloton, a mechanical and bike change for world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) saw him dropped from the peloton and facing a substantial chase back on, but he made it back to the bunch and his teammates without too much trouble.

The longest climb of the day, the Valpiana, passed without much action, with the breakaway riders managing their efforts and keeping the gap stable towards the 150km to go mark. On the long descent, however, the breakaway actually managed to grow their advantage over the peloton, stretching the gap out to three minutes for the first time all day as the still 14-strong group took on the long flat before the next climb.

Things were certainly not slow in the peloton heading into the final 120km, but teams and riders seemed to be just making sure they didn't do too much, too soon with the decisive climbs all still to come.

It did not take too long for the pace to kick back up in the bunch, though, and the gap started slowly falling again on the Giovenzana climb as UAE lined up at the front of the peloton and started burning through riders.

With 90km to go, the break briefly split apart, and whilst they reunited relatively quickly, it was the first sign of the leaders perhaps getting ready to attack and take opportunities. The long, flat, lake-side stretch before the Madonna del Ghisallo gave the break a chance to reset and regroup, though the peloton were winding up towards full pace in their pursuit.

The break hit the Madonna del Ghisallo 2:30 ahead of the peloton, with the stronger climbers quickly coming to the fore and O'Connor settling the early pace. His efforts saw Tiberi among the first riders to be dropped, and soon hardly anyone could hold onto the Australian's wheel, with him and Leemreize pulling out a gap on the early slopes. Leonard was able to pace back up to them, making it three in the lead, but Leemreize soon dropped back as the leaders' gap fell back below two minutes.

That shrinking of the gap was because, just as had happened in the break, the bunch hitting the climb signalled the arrival of the favourites and climbers at the front of the peloton; no one was quite attacking, but Red Bull and UAE were both battling for supremacy on the front of the group.

O'Connor and Leonard were rejoined by five riders from the break halfway up the climb, but the seven leaders were now less than a minute and a half ahead of the bunch, led by Red Bull's Giulio Pellizzari.

The attacks began near the top when Louis Barre (Visma-Lease a Bike) led out a big move from Matteo Jorgenson, with his compatriots Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) and McNulty on his wheel, plus XDS Astana's Christian Scaroni. The quartet went clear over the top of the climb, and though they didn't have a huge gap on the peloton, it left Evenepoel, Red Bull and Decathlon with work to do on the descent.

Red Bull enlisted Primož Roglič to help in the chase, and with 50km to go, the attackers – with Masnada from the break now tagging along too – were 13 seconds ahead of the main group, with the leaders another 50 seconds up the road. The attackers were caught only a few kilometres later, though, and there was a brief rest as the favourites weighed up their next moves.

This slight lull saw the leaders' gap go back out, and they still had 1:20 with 35km to go as the race entered the finishing circuit and the final three climbs. After looking strong, Simmons had a poorly timed mechanical at the start of the circuit and dropped out of the reduced bunch and faced a tough chase back on.

All the favourite teams were amassed at the front of the peloton, but there was still a lot of work to be done to actually bring the leaders back if the big names were to contest the finish. On the first time up the San Fermo della Battaglia climb, Pellizzari hit the front once again to wind things up for Evenepoel, with McNulty, Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5), Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and Seixas behind them.

Pellizzari paced to the top of the climb, and his efforts took a big chunk out of the leaders' advantage, though they were still working hard up front to try and give themselves as big a chance as possible of holding on. The gap sat at 40 seconds with 20km remaining.

On the Civiglio climb, Leonard pushed on up ahead to be the final survivor of the break, but the favourites were hot on his heels as Paul Seixas made his first serious move towards the top, which reeled Leonard back in but – more crucially – saw Evenepoel struggling to hold on at the back of the group.

Seixas' move was not explosive, but a steady winding up of his speed was an effort that only Pidcock and Ciccone could follow, with Evenepoel and Del Toro noticeably off the pace. It didn't take long for Seixas to drop his companions, too, and the young Frenchman went solo with 18km remaining. He went over the top of the climb with a gap of 25 seconds on Ciccone and Mas, which was not insurmountable, but Seixas looked much stronger than the riders trying to chase him down, and his gap only grew as he settled into his rhythm.

Ciccone and Mas weren't working well together behind, so Mas pushed on solo without the Italian, but even that was fairly futile as he was still nearly a minute down on Seixas with 5km to go. That gap meant the Frenchman was able to savour his victory as he soloed to the line, capping a phenomenal season with an historic first Monument victory.

Mas rolled in for second just ahead of Ciccone, whilst Evenepoel sprinted it out for fourth from the large chasing group, but ultimately could not live up to his favourite status.
