title: Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest
author: Sirin Kale
text:
Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry

A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.

In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences , including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.

The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.

Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery.

A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.

Chan was first arrested in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.

After Chan’s devices were searched by police as part of this investigation, they discovered that he was a prolific sexual offender, with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, north London , including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison.

The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate.

In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025.

Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children.

Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children.

LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently.

After Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work after the Bright Horizons investigation. The review concluded in November 2025, and Camden council subsequently commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how Chan was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role.

The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.

In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.

There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information.

It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery.

A spokesperson for Camden council said: “Children deserve the best care in a safe environment and the ongoing independent local child safeguarding review into this case presents a pivotal opportunity to prevent abuse like this from happening again. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information.

“We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.”…

title: K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
author: Terrence O’Brien
text:
Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.

Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.

Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single “ Nobody ” was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009.

In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards.

Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid , in 2025. This year she released the single “ Forever July ,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos.

My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it.

The Samsung Galaxy series. It has made my work environment so much easier. Team Galaxyyyyyy!

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

These days, you can transfer all the apps and data from your previous device, so I don’t really have to install anything separately. But if that process didn’t exist, I’d probably install KakaoTalk, a messaging app, first.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

I have so many unnecessary photos and screenshots in my gallery. I wish there were a feature that could recognize similar or duplicate photos and group them together, so I could delete them all at once.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

Notion. I use it a lot because I work on many group projects. It’s convenient, but it takes quite a long time to get used to. I think the UI could use some improvement.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Four: Notion, Google Drive, YouTube, and Claude.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I don’t really use social media that much, but I think I use Instagram and X the most.

Videos of people getting their ears cleaned on YouTube.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

I’m not really good with technology, but I think the Samsung Z Fold 8 that I’m using right now is probably my favorite device. I often need to work on documents or edit videos while I’m on the go, and it’s incredibly convenient. I can work with both hands on a wide screen, and it’s surprisingly light. It’s exactly the kind of device I’ve always needed.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

MapleStory by Nexon. I played it when I was in elementary school, and even after becoming an adult, I would sometimes play the mobile version. The graphics really bring back memories of my childhood.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Stranger Things 5 and Game of Thrones 8 .

“Tail.” It’s a song that still gets me excited every time I perform it live. When I hold my breath, the audience holds their breath too, and when I explode, they explode with me. It creates this really unique experience.

“You Can’t Sit with Us.” It was the first song where I ever tried rapping. But the lyrics and even my voice were terrible.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

Always stay humble. You should never let yourself become arrogant.

I really love ice cream. Korean summers are shockingly hot, so it’s hard to survive without ice cream. I absolutely love Salt & Straw’s Salted Caramel Waffle Cone, but there’s nothing quite like it in Korea.

I find a small space to organize my thoughts.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

I say “No?” out loud. For example, if I start thinking to myself, “I can’t do this,” I immediately say “No?” out loud.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

When I’m shooting, I leave my phone with my manager. Even during short breaks, I barely look at my phone. But I’ve never actually gone somewhere without my phone.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

The Senses of an Everydayist , a new essay collection by lyricist Kim Eana. She sent me a copy as a gift when it was published, but I believe there’s something meaningful about personally buying and reading someone’s creative work, so I bought a copy online.

Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore GP pole
author: Josh Suttill
text:
Max Verstappen’s perfect Singapore weekend continued as he claimed pole position for the grand prix, beating the Ferraris in Formula 1 qualifying.

Verstappen’s first Q3 flying lap - a 1m31.373s - ended up being good enough to top qualifying, following on from his sprint race pole and victory.

Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari was his closest challenger, setting a lap 0.054s slower than Verstappen’s. Lewis Hamilton made it two Ferraris in the top three, just 0.069s adrift of Leclerc.

Kimi Antonelli will line up on the second row alongside Hamilton, having been fourth-quickest in the upgraded Mercedes.

The McLaren drivers, who collided in the sprint race, will share the third row.

Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were fifth and seventh in qualifying with George Russell between them in the older-spec Mercedes, but Russell will move to the back of the grid with an engine penalty.

Pierre Gasly won F1’s midfield fight in qualifying, qualifying eighth (which is set to become seventh on the grid) and beating the Racing Bulls duo of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad.

Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg was the quickest driver knocked out in Q2, 0.182s away from a place in Q3.

Haas drivers Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon were 12th and 13th ahead of Carlos Sainz’s Williams, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto and Alpine’s Franco Colapinto, over a second slower than team-mate Gasly.

Both Aston Martins fell in the first stage of qualifying after Fernando Alonso reported a turbo issue, which he thinks means his team should change his power unit for the race.

He qualified 17th, just ahead of Alex Albon’s Williams and still seven tenths clear of team-mate Lance Stroll, just as he was in sprint qualifying.

Sergio Perez led Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas, the pair the two slowest drivers to set a lap in qualifying.

Isack Hadjar’s nightmare Saturday in Singapore continued as he ground to a halt before he could even set a timed lap in Q1.

Hadjar managed to return his Red Bull to the garage, then came out again and encountered an issue again. He will start among the penalised drivers at the back of the field on Sunday.

title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as ‘thanks’ for Trump diesel deal, Zelenskyy says
author: Oliver Holmes
text:
Ukrainian president says money from fuel sales will intensify war as European leaders reiterate support for Kyiv

Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal cut by Donald Trump with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, accusing Washington of helping fund Moscow’s war.

The Ukrainian president has expressed repeated outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November midterm elections where the cost of fuel is a key voter issue.

The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.

He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 15 people, including three children.

“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.

“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.

There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.

In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.

“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​ Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.

The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.

“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.

Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationship with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine .

The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.

Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.

Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.

title: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
author: Terrence O’Brien
text:
Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’

Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’

After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed “ unintended model actions ,” including submitting a false tip regarding an unsolved murder, that led to the decision.

Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these.

The ability to gain access to the live internet , even when models were supposed to be operating in isolation, has been an ongoing issue for AI companies. Many incidents, including the Hugging Face attack, involved agents that were supposed to be denied access to the internet. Yet, in case after case, the agents found creative solutions to bypass those restrictions. Physically removing internet access would certainly improve security around AI testing, but it would also limit its usefulness .

The report also amounts to an admission that Anthropic is often unaware of what its agents are doing and does not have a reliable system for monitoring their behavior. Cutting off internet access is just the latest action the company has taken to try and rein in its agents, including temporarily pausing training its frontier models.

title: Stewards rule Piastri shares blame for Norris clash
author: Josh Suttill
text:
Formula 1’s Singapore Grand Prix stewards determined that both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri contributed to their last-lap sprint race collision, so ruled that no further action was necessary.

The stewards said Piastri hadn’t expected Norris to overtake him, but he "noticed [Norris] on the inside and attempted to leave space".

"[Norris] said that he saw an opportunity to overtake and said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of [Piastri] prior to the apex, and therefore expected to be left space.

"As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated, so he had to use the inside kerb and braked, and a collision occurred.

"The stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision.

"Therefore, the stewards determined to take no further action."

Norris is right that he had his front axle ahead of the mirror of Piastri’s sister car at the apex of Turn 5, so he satisfies that aspect of F1’s racing rules.

But it does not appear Piastri - who was caught unawares by the divebomb - had means of leaving more space at that corner; so once he turned in, a collision became inevitable.

Given the stewards stated "both drivers had contributed to the incident", we can infer that Piastri’s not anticipating the overtake and leaving enough space is what he did wrong - whereas Norris was ambitious with his move and had to climb onto the inside kerb to try to complete it.

The start of Norris’s interview with F1 broadcaster Viaplay after the sprint race made his feelings clear.

Norris was asked: "You'll surely always want to finish as high as possible, but it’s also a sprint, P4 and P5 and it was your team-mate in front of you... Wasn’t it too unnecessary, that move?"

He replied: "What, to go for a big gap? To overtake?". He followed up: "What's the title name of the race?"

The interviewer replied, "sprint", to which Norris said: "Sprint. What’s [the word] after sprint?" - "race" came the reply.

Norris smiled: "Wow! Good job. It’s a race".

"We were just stuck the whole race and the last lap there was a big opportunity into [Turn] 5 so I went for it," Norris said in the media pen.

"The gap closed a bit more than I would have liked and obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing - so I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one. But it was a big gap so I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team."

Piastri said "it’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, not that bothered either way, just a lot of work for the team to get both cars fixed, just a shame for the team".

Meanwhile, Liam Lawson, having been shown a replay of the incident by Sky Sports F1’s Karun Chandhok, mused: "On the last lap, it’s not for many points; I don't think it's worth it".

Perez dodges serving penalty for Stroll clash

There was a slightly unusual decision made in the assessment of another of the sprint’s incidents.

Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll collided on the opening lap of the race when Perez tried to pass on the inside of the Turn 16 right-hander.

The stewards felt Stroll had turned in reasonably for the corner and Perez was predominantly to blame after having a lock-up.

They considered the tricky conditions reasonable mitigation and wanted to issue Perez with a five-second penalty instead of the usual 10.

But Perez retired from the race - and according to the stewards a five-second penalty does not typically convert to a grid drop.

Had it been a 10-second penalty, this would be different. So Perez escapes sanction for the clash.

title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
text:
US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel into the global market.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.

"Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, said any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war.

Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.

That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

The BBC understands the Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large.

An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.

Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.

Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.

But on Friday Zelensky defended the strikes, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".

"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear.

But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.

What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on what reimbursement the US is providing Russia in return for the release of diesel.

With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.

Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline, and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.

Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

title: Things from the Aaron Boone era that I’m sick of watching
author: Matt Ferenchick
text:
This year’s ALDS sweep at the hands of the Rays felt like a culmination for the Aaron Boone era Yankees. I’m not sure it will be a culmination of his managerial tenure as I could definitely see the team keeping him, but those three games felt like everything that has gone wrong in a Yankees’ playoff exit from 2018 to now all rolled into one. There were mental mistakes, sloppy play, and bats going cold all at once.

I think it would be unfair to say that Boone hasn’t grown at all since taking the job. Early in his tenure, I used to get frustrated by him sticking with a pitcher too long trying to steal an extra out or two. These days, it seems pretty rare that those instances happen. However, any growth from him is overshadowed by the frustration that I share with many other Yankee fans.

In watching this year’s playoff defeat , my mind couldn’t help but keep going over the things that went wrong that I could see coming, because all of Boone’s teams seem to suffer in these ways. Whether or not the Yankees do bring Aaron Boone back, I personally am out, and it would take a massive change of fortune to change that. Here are the reasons why.

For one, his teams seem to play with just no sense of fundamentals. I am an analytically-inclined fan, so when I say this, I don’t meant that they don’t bunt enough or that they need to learn to go the other way and hit singles, because I think there are logical reasons that make it easier said than done against the pitchers of today. However, there are some baseball things that happen in the heat of the moment of a game that don’t make sense no matter your way of thinking.

Austin Wells getting thrown out try to stretch a double into a triple in Game 1 of the ALDS is the perfect example. “Don’t make the last out of the inning at third base” is a longtime baseball axiom that makes perfect sense. With two outs, you can’t score on a sacrifice fly or any other kind of productive out, so those 90 feet matter way less than just having a chance with a runner in scoring position. Yet in the heat of the game, Wells seemingly wasn’t even thinking about that, never mind the fact that he ran through Luis Rojas’ stop sign too.

I feel like I regularly watch the Yankees allow opposing runners to take extra bases because a fielder tries for an out at home that has like a five percent chance at happening rather than throwing ahead of the runner, holding them, and living to fight for another day. Or, an infielder will try and make a rushed and/or spectacular throw to try and complete a double play leading to an error, and a runner getting an extra base (à la Jazz Chisholm Jr. in Game 2 ). I know it’s probably hard to think about these things in the moment and your instincts will kick in to some degree, but it feels like the Yankees regularly disadvantage themselves by going to the spectacular instead of sticking to basics.

Relatededly, I have another issue with the defense in general. Anthony Volpe went from winning a Gold Glove as a rookie to looking like a shortstop novice in just two seasons. It’s cost the Yankees some playoff games, including the infamous 2024 World Series Game 5 meltdown. Again, errors are something that are going to occur no matter what, but the Boone Yankees have been so sloppy so often.

That sloppiness also almost always comes to a head during an almost annual mid-season — usually around June or July — swoon.

Another baseball saying is that every team wins 50 and loses 50, and your season is decided by what you do in the rest of the games. For the most part, that holds true and I don’t think there’s any manager who could’ve snapped their fingers and won 110 games with any of Boone’s Yankees teams. Every team is going to slump. However, why is it that every Boone team will start off hot and then go through about a month where they appear to forget how to play baseball?

This year, they went 12-14 in June. If you expand that out to a couple days either side of the month, they had a 15-20 stretch. In 2025, they were under .500 in all of June and July. They were under .500 in July 2024, and that includes a five-game winning streak at the end of the month. They were on pace for 122 wins in mid-June 2022 and ended up winning under 100.

Again, I recognize that every team is going to have some slumps. The MLB-best Brewers were just barely over .500 after April and ended up with 103 wins. No team is going to put up exactly even .600 winning percentages every month — even the 1998 Yankees played a few ticks below that pace in September. However, I would appreciate if the Yankees stop having a stretch that obviously foreshadows what is going to happen that October.

Another issue that has played out in the postseason, but sometimes appears in the regular season as well is that the Boone Yankees’ teams never get the last laugh. I don’t mean this just in a “they haven’t won the World Series” sense, but they always seem to be the team that ends with with egg on their face.

In 2020, they got into it with the Rays after Aroldis Chapman airmailed a pitch over Mike Brosseau’s head, leading to a verbal back and forth between the two teams, on the field and in the media. What happens that October? The Yankees lose to the Rays after … Mike Brosseau homers off Aroldis Chapman.

In a 2021 Subway Series game, Francisco Lindor made allusions to what he perceived as the Yankees’ stealing signs. Giancarlo Stanton chirped him back after he hit a home run, leading to the benches clearing . However, what ended up deciding the game? Lindor’s third homer of the game.

Beyond just losing every postseason under Boone, the Yankees constantly end up the butt of jokes, and frankly I’m done with it.

title: Will Warner Bros. kill Skydance — or will David Ellison kill Warner Bros?
author: Nilay Patel
text:
Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at and host of the podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.

Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.

There are some grand ambitions here, but the reality is that acquiring Warner never goes well for anyone. AOL failed, AT&T failed, and Discovery failed — although it did succeed in flipping these assets to Skydance. So I wanted to ask Peter if he thinks the Ellisons and Skydance have a real shot at succeeding where so many companies before them have hit the rocks.

Okay: Peter Kafka on Warner Bros. and Skydance. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Peter Kafka, you’re the chief correspondent at Business Insider, and you’re the host of the podcast, our sister podcast here on the Vox Media Podcast Network. Welcome back to

Thanks for having me. It’s big media day again!

A big media day. It’s an auspicious day, as my parents would say. It is the day that the Warner-Paramount merger closes. We’ve all been calling it Warner Mount, but I’m told this company will instead

Every time I see the word Skydance, I assume it is foreign-owned, which is maybe true in some way.

Another way to think of it is that there are iconic names in Hollywood. Paramount is such an iconic name that Viacom turned itself into Paramount years ago. Warner Bros. is a legendary studio. Let’s get rid of those names. Let’s add Skydance, which no one’s ever heard of.

Let’s just start at the start. There was Paramount. There’s Warner Bros. The deal closes today. That is all going to be a new company called Skydance. Is Skydance just a holding company? Are we as consumers meant to know that this thing exists?

I think for the near term, you’re still gonna think of companies like Paramount, Warner Bros., and HBO as brands you know, but this is going to be one company. They’re going to merge everything. They’re likely going to merge the streaming services, Paramount and HBO, into a thing, not right away, but eventually. So I do think Skydance will be a name that consumers will probably know at some point.

I just have to ask, what are the chances that HBO Max will be rebranded yet again into Skydance?

There’s probably gonna be some branding stuff. Not again. In the near term, because this is still a cable TV company, there are actually some limits on what these guys can do with their brands and their services. And they won’t come out and say, “We’re gonna mush this stuff together.”

But there’s likely to be one mega streaming service, and maybe you can get HBO separately, or maybe you can only get HBO or only Paramount. Still, it’s gonna be one thing, and one movie studio. It’s all gonna get mushed together, and it’s all gonna be run by David Ellison.

David Ellison is just the latest to believe that he can buy Warner Bros. and make something good happen. I have joked many times on this show that maybe the only antitrust policy this country needs is to make it illegal to buy Warner Bros., and that would just solve a lot of problems. Why does he think he will be successful?

Well, his dad’s the eighth richest man in the world, so that’s not nothing.

That Oracle stock is tied up in a bunch of AI stuff. It’s moving up and down.

We can talk about that. But one, that means that he literally has the money to buy this, and two, that this is a public company kind of in name only. David Ellison and Larry Ellison, his father, control this company effectively. They don’t really need to worry that much about equity shareholders. Debt’s a different issue.

And he’s 43. He’s got a long run backed by tens of billions of dollars of his father’s money to take a stab at this. And as you said, he will not be the first person to do this. There’s a long list of failures. I think maybe that’s appealing to guys like him. It’s like, “Everyone else is dumb. I’m the smart guy who’s gonna figure it out.”

“Everyone else is dumb, and I’m smarter than everyone else is,” is very appealing. But that long list of failures, if you just look at it — they’re all shaped like this idea. We’re gonna take iconic Warner Bros. content, we’re gonna marry it to new distribution, we’re gonna reduce the overhead and costs and decadence of Hollywood. Where does new revenue come from?

There’s no plan for new revenue. There’s no plan for new revenue. Right now it’s shrinking; it’s cutting costs. It’s when we merge these two companies together, we’re gonna save $6 billion over the next three years. We promise that most of that’s not gonna come from layoffs, but a lot of it’s gonna come from layoffs.

These are companies that have had many, many rounds of layoffs prior to this. And you could argue, well, there’s probably not that much more to cut. I think reasonably you could say, look, if you combine two big streaming operations, two big studio operations, there probably is stuff [to cut]. You can probably sell off some real estate. You probably don’t need all the executives you currently have. There’s some savings there. But how do you grow? No idea. And no one’s really articulated that.

Growth is required for a couple of reasons here. One, yes, there are going to be shareholders; people will be looking at it. There’s David Ellison’s ego. Then there’s debt. This deal is levered to the max, right?

Eighty billion dollars [in debt]. Eight zero. More important than the number is the reason that David Ellison was able to buy Warner Bros. was that the last owner couldn’t deal with the debt that he took on to buy the company. And that was a mere $43 or $50 billion, depending on who was counting. This is David Zaslav, the former CEO of Warner Bros. Discovery, who spent his entire tenure running that company telling Wall Street that, yes, he was gonna get the debt down, and that was his main focus, and debt, debt, debt, reduce, reduce, reduce.

I mean, he did reduce some debt, but he never convinced Wall Street that he had a plan to grow. Wall Street gave up on this company years ago, which is why when David Ellison decided he wanted to buy it, the stock was, like, seven bucks or something like that. Eventually bought it for, you know, many, many times that.

And now David Zaslav is considered — or he considers himself — a genius for selling the company at such a high price. You could also argue, as someone told me yesterday, that a unicorn sort of manifested itself and allowed David Zaslav to exit the situation he had put himself into.

I don’t know who the next unicorn will be for this company if David Ellison at some point decides, “Ugh, actually this is a lot of debt and a lot of pain. I don’t wanna do this anymore.”

I want to come back to that because I have a little bit of a conspiracy theory. It’s a little bit supported by the attitudes of some of the players here, but we’ll come back around. Even the previous owner, AT&T, which is remarkable that AT&T was the… Somewhere in this chain of ownership, AT&T owned Warner.

They could not deal with these assets. Their plan was to distribute Warner content on AT&T phones, which never made any sense. But they were a more aggressive owner.

It also wasn’t really their plan. Their plan was, “Hey, Netflix is a really valuable company. The stock is very high. We’re this boring telecoms company. Our stock is not moving. What if we owned a [version of] Netflix? I bet Wall Street would reward us as a high-flying tech company all of a sudden.” And Wall Street didn’t.

Within a couple of years, AT&T said, “Uh, oh yeah, no, we’re out of this.” And yes, they had said a bunch of stuff about mobile, connectivity, ads, and targeting, and none of that ever went anywhere

I will never forget covering their antitrust case when they had to get approval for that deal. They that they had a vision of the future. The judge in that case, in the appeals court opinion, wrote, “This is a vision deal.” And I thought, “We’re doomed.” Like, I don’t know what’s going on in our judiciary [system].

I want a Vision deal. How do I get one of those?

I don’t know. I was like, “I don’t know what that is at all.”

So, we have a lot of debt. The FCC had to on foreign ownership. There’s 49 percent of the money from the Gulf in this company. Then there’s the Oracle of it. I’ve always wondered what amounts to an AI stock for a media stock, especially right now.

But the AI trade is a little shakier than it was before. Oracle has been punished a little bit for this deal. What do you make of that? Is that an effective backstop?

I don’t know if Oracle was punished for this deal. I mean, there was a period a year ago when Larry Ellison’s net worth was double what it is now. And you could say, “Well, that was just a weird AI blip.” It’s still a very highly valued company. He is still the eighth richest man in the world because of his Oracle holdings.

Wall Street is a little bit nervous now about the fact that Larry Ellison’s source of wealth is Oracle. He’s borrowing from Oracle. He has backstopped the Warner Bros. deal by pledging to come up with $40 or $50 billion if he needs to. And there is a question of, like, all right, not only is Oracle sort of intimately tied into this new media company, but Oracle’s also entirely dependent on one AI company, OpenAI, for its new plan.

So late in life — Larry Ellison is 82 years old — he’s decided he’s kind of putting the entire company on AI and on OpenAI specifically. And while he’s not doing that, he’s going to use some of that money to fund his son’s media empire. I don’t know if it’s rickety, but it’s definitely a question mark.

I open Instagram. Right now my Instagram algorithm is crazy because I keep looking for Instagram’s tolerance for copyright infringement, and it is high. Instagram has basically unlimited tolerance for copyright infringement. Mark Zuckerberg is posting deepfake memes of himself doing rap videos now.

These are details. By the way, Nilay, you know who’s figured out the Instagram and Reels algorithm? You! I get so much Nilay front-facing video. You’re very good at it. You should consider being an influencer. You have figured this out.

I try to deeply understand the things that are gonna kill me, and so that’s… We’re just looking at that one, and I’m looking at my daughter. I’m like, “I should know what’s going on here.”

All this AI makes it impossibly cheap and easy to just take the IP from these movie studios. I watched a video last night of the Heath Ledger Joker and the Christian Bale Batman just doing a Justin Bieber video, and then I was served 5,000 more videos like this.

That’s the OpenAI business. They’re gonna destroy the creative foundations that make the IP valuable that Warner Bros. makes, and somewhere in there is a big problem that I can’t quite figure out.

Yeah, I think it maybe is simpler than that. You’re right, there are all kinds of copyright issues. The value of your library may be much less if someone can just take it without paying you. But I think the bigger issue for David Ellison and anyone in the media business is that what you really want is people’s attention.

You have this company saddled with $80 billion in debt because it makes all kinds of entertainment, really expensive movies, all this sort of stuff, and now anyone can make anything that will at least get your attention for a few seconds on Instagram and TikTok. And so there’s this flood of stuff, whether it’s copyright infringement or not, it’s just stuff that the David Ellisons of the world have to contend with because your daughter and my kids might easily watch that stuff rather than the original movie.

I think that is sort of the existential problem [not just] for Skydance, but every media company today.…

title: Cockroach Party Leaders Detained to Stop Protests
text: Indian authorities detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka ahead of a planned demonstration against a contentious revision of voter rolls. Police imposed sweeping restrictions in the national capital to stop supporters and allies from gathering for the youth-led protest. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
author: Michael Sainato
text:
Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote

The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference.

The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October.

Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote.

“The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028.

“These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.”

In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election.

Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023.

He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.

Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits.

Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.

title: Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after Mercedes driver George Russell crashed out of the lead.

Russell was leading in tricky conditions, with half the track dry and half wet, when he got a little too wide at the final corner at the end of the first lap.

He lost control of his Mercedes, which spun across the track into the inside wall, before bouncing back again to the outside, the rest of the field somehow avoiding him.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second having made a superb start from sixth on the grid with team-mate Charles Leclerc third.

A final-lap collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri at Turn Five promoted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli to fourth place.

In combination with Russell's retirement, that extends the Italian's championship lead to 89 points.

A chaotic race saw the start delayed by 30 minutes by a tropical downpour, and then Verstappen navigating a safety car period following Russell's accident, a restart, and initial pressure from Hamilton to eventually ease away into a comfortable lead.

It was the Dutchman's second Formula 1 win in seven days, after his maiden victory this season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the first time he has won in Singapore.

The rain before the start hit only parts of the track. The second sector stayed dry while the first sector, particularly Turns Two and Three, were soaking wet with standing water.

Once the rain abated, the field did two laps behind a safety car to check conditions before racing began with a standing start.

Russell gave himself a golden opportunity to breathe some life into his almost-extinguished title hopes when he beat Verstappen off the line and took the lead into the first corner.

But after leading the first lap, he made a mistake at the final corner.

Russell said: "I just misjudged it, got more power than I was expecting from the battery, got a little wider than I expected and touched the white line. Rule number one in the wet is don't touch the white line. Very silly mistake."

That left Verstappen in front, with Hamilton behind. But after the seven-time champion pursued his erstwhile 2021 title rival for a few laps, the Red Bull began to ease away and was clearly in control, leading Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli.

With overtaking difficult around Marina Bay, the field was static until the closing stages.

Leclerc was struggling, and he began to be caught by the McLarens and Antonelli.

Norris had been pressuring Piastri for some laps before the Australian also began to close in on Leclerc, and Antonelli, struggling with oversteer in the early laps, picked up the pace.

On the final lap, Norris made a better exit out of Turn Three and saw an opportunity to try to pass Piastri at Turn Five, but Piastri defended his position robustly, the cars touched, and spun in unison.

Norris was initially far enough alongside to make a legitimate passing attempt, but having apparently tried to back out of the move, not so at the apex to satisfy the driving standards rules.

But the criticism of Norris will be that he miscalculated the risk-reward, that it was an ill-advised, marginal move against his team-mate for little gain - a point was at stake - and none for the team, as it would have not changed their collective points total.

The stewards investigated the incident but took no action on the basis that both drivers had contributed to the incident.

Piastri, who hit the barriers, was out on the spot, but Norris was able to keep going, although he fell down to eighth, behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.

title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’
author: Helena Horton and Michael Goodier
text:
Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding

When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.

Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England .

But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story.

Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset.

The businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt.

As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs.

And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge.

Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.

The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50.

Bekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room.

He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head.

Hugh Thomas, a food writer from Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.”

Some, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs.

Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomed a cage of endangered red squirrels . But there, too, lay a problem.

The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds.

Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.”

While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds.

People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.

Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”

The worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”. The local authority declared an emergency that evening.

Villagers have also set up a petition against the spraying of pesticides on the Newt’s farmland.

The model and actor Gabriella Wilde, who also lives locally, said: “I was surprised and a little disappointed to learn that they are using such harmful chemicals in their farming operations. That is certainly not the image they project to their guests and local fans. Is it really necessary, especially given how many local farms are making great strides in moving away from old school harmful practices, and towards more nature friendly farming?”…

title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
author: Hayden Field
text:
Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.

Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company’s new AI agent Dots — and told the crowd that the company wants to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta’s Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users’ data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw — with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”

In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.

Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”

But though Muse topped the App Store charts and, per Apptopia, gained 600,000 daily active users in the US within weeks, Meta’s promises seem to have fallen short. Although data is isolated from other users, and the company plans to introduce a way “to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM” later this year, Meta itself can still access the data. A security researcher quickly exposed a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of Muse (which has since been patched), raising fears of outside attacks. Multiple serious security issues reportedly cropped up at the last minute before launch , one of which could have allowed users to access Meta’s own internal databases, per 404 Media .

Muse also appears to liberally collect (and in some cases, hand out) data. It defaults to allowing Meta to train models on what users put into it, though it’s possible to opt out. An Inc. reporter complained that Muse uploaded and read his private messages without him asking it to, and a YouTuber said it had offered his address to a stranger via Marketplace — in both cases, Muse was functioning apparently as intended, but the user didn’t realize how far it would go. The platform creates “detailed profiles of all your friends and family,” as Wired reported. None of this is necessarily unexpected from Meta, but it certainly doesn’t back up the idea that Muse is uniquely privacy- or security-conscious.

OpenAI seized on this fact when announcing Dots in late September. Alexander Embiricos, OpenAI’s Codex product lead, said onstage at DevDay that OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” and CEO Sam Altman demonstrated ways that people could exert control over their individual Dots, such as setting a rule that it should never make a purchase over a certain dollar amount. “I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” said Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, adding that “launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid.”

Altman himself also pushed the privacy angle at DevDay. To court business customers, executives presented a framework allowing enterprises to have “stronger controls” over their data and zero data retention policy options (meaning no data is stored on OpenAI servers). Indeed, so far, there haven’t been many privacy scandals with Dots — although since it’s only available on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers, there are also likely fewer people using it.

People may still not feel comfortable giving OpenAI their personal data, in part simply because AI agents require so much of it. For instance, The Verge ’s Allison Johnson felt uncomfortable typing in her bank information when the bot asked as part of a relevant task (Muse has a Stripe integration to take care of that).

Not all companies are making privacy promises, of course. Instinct was publicly criticized for reportedly overly-broad terms of service that gave it unfettered access to data; since then, the company seems to have made adjustments. For now, AI labs seem to be counting on a three-part approach to popularizing AI agent use with the general public: Make them useful, make them cute and disarming to help offset the creepiness, and make promises about privacy — and hope they hold up.

title: LG’s RGB LED TV is good for certain situations, but an OLED is better
author: John Higgins
text:
A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.﻿

A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.﻿

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.

The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. It has a more traditional remote shape instead of the curved wand of previous versions. As with all LG TVs, the MRGB95B runs on webOS. It runs quickly, but I find it less intuitive to navigate than Google TV, Apple TV, or Roku. It supports all of the major streaming apps.

Some color inaccuracy out of the box Very distracting reflective screen More blooming than competitors

Speaking of software, a quick note: LG has recently come under increased scrutiny after a video from Gamers Nexus showed security vulnerabilities and continuous audio recording on its TVs, which LG has denied . When setting up the MRGB95B, it’s only necessary to accept the terms of use and privacy policy if you want to use webOS. Otherwise, as with any TV, it can be disconnected from the internet, although an external streaming device would be needed for any streaming services (I use an Apple TV 4K, myself).

OK, moving on. So, why buy an RGB LED TV?

RGB LED TVs use zones of individual red, green, and blue LEDs as backlights as opposed to a field of white or blue LEDs that rely on a color filter or quantum dots to create the colors that reach our eyes. RGB LED TVs have a color filter, too, but since the backlight is already creating color based on what’s needed onscreen, the color filter doesn’t need to work as hard to dial that in. It allows for higher color brightness and the ability to display more colors.

LG (and Samsung) use the term Micro RGB to describe the technology, while others say Mini RGB LED. And while the LG and Samsung RGBs are reportedly smaller (although neither has confirmed the exact size), it doesn’t directly translate into more zones or better performance over Mini RGB.

As with all of the RGB LED TVs I’ve seen this year, the 95B gets very bright — I measured a peak of 4,011 nits in HDR Filmmaker mode — allowing it to deliver an impactful image even in a sunlit living room. And in a dark room, the highlights in scenes from The Meg really pop. At the other end of the spectrum, though, the LG struggles a bit. Near-black shadow detail, such as the corners of the living room and kitchen of Sapper Morton’s home at the beginning of Blade Runner 2049 , is difficult to see. And when there are bright moments within a dark portion of the screen — subtitles are a good example — the LG exhibits more blooming than I’ve seen on other RGB LED TVs.

HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC)

Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Atmos FlexConnect, Dolby Digital, Auracast

Gaming features: VRR, ALLM, Game Optimizer, G-Sync compatible

The LG 95B can display really vibrant colors thanks to the RGB LED technology. It’s able to cover 100 percent of the P3 color gamut (which is what’s used for films) and nearly 90 percent of the larger BT.2020 color area. But even in Filmmaker mode out of the box, those colors still show visible accuracy issues. Overall, the TV leans toward light blue, so white clouds have a slight blue tint to them and skin tones are cooler than they should be.

After a few days living with the LG MRGB95B, I got used to the slightly blue image (although it was still noticeable). A $3,600 TV in 2026 shouldn’t have the inaccuracies on the MRGB95B.

While the TV performs well in a bright room during the day, when the sun goes down and the lamps turn on, they can wreak havoc on the image. The 95B’s glossy coating is one of the most reflective I’ve seen in a long time. In moderately lit rooms, a lamp or ceiling light directly reflected on the screen causes rainbows to dance across the image. It’s not as bad when the scene is bright, such as the scorching desert of Arrakis in Dune , but once we enter the dark corridors of House Harkonnen, the reflections become incredibly noticeable.

Viewing angles are always a problem for LED TVs — RGB or not — and that’s evident on the LG, too. When only moderately off-axis, the colors become washed out, losing their vibrancy for anyone who’s sitting off to the side.

In a vacuum, the MRGB95B is a good TV for certain situations. It’s really bright and stands up to ambient light well (just avoid having ceiling, wall, or standing lights reflected on the screen), and the colors are vibrant if not totally accurate out of the box. But it doesn’t hold up against other TVs. The Sony Bravia 7 II (which you can find $1,300 cheaper at 75 inches) has better color accuracy and handles reflections better. And the Hisense UR9 performs comparably for less money, too.

But the real competition comes from within LG itself. The LG G6 OLED is only a few hundred dollars more than the MRGB95B, as is the Samsung S95H, and both of those TVs offer significantly better performance with superior color accuracy and viewing angles. The OLEDs don’t get quite as bright, but since they can turn off light at the pixel level, contrast is remarkable and there’s zero blooming.…

title: On the Yankees’ playoff failures and the agony of apathy
author: Joshua Diemert
text:
I try very hard to fight back against apathy. In politics, the economy, media, the world begs for your apathy. Don’t make a fuss, let it all just happen. It’s all going According to Plan. The state apparatus depends on your apathy. Do not give them that gift.

And yet, not quite 48 hours after the Yankees once again lost in the ALDS, lost to a team seeded higher than them, lost to a team that is just so fundamentally annoying that thinking about them raises my blood pressure a point or two…I don’t feel much at all.

I’ve always tried to hedge my reactions to bad sports news. The Don LeGreca-style rants make for good radio and some of the longer, more unhinged comments we get here are fun to scroll past, but at the end of the day I consume baseball for my own entertainment. Letting yourself get mad over something you say you enjoy while having 0 control over it hasn’t made a whole lot of sense to me. Let sports lift you up, not press you down.

And true to form, I’m not mad about the 2026 Yankees. I’m beige. The Yankees dogwalked the Red Sox last week only to find themselves canine-ized by the Rays, swept out of the ALDS in what’s actually a worse result than last year. (They lasted a whole four games against the Blue Jays!) Aaron Boone put the worst leadoff hitter in baseball atop the lineup, telling us that he liked the potential for action on the basepaths ahead of the only batter who showed up in the series, and that leadoff hitter went 0-for-5 as the team died—with him as the final out—because of course he did.

I don’t quite know why I’m so numb to all of this. The Yankees won 93 games, the second-best record in the AL, without the game’s best player, while actively rehabbing three pitchers in their starting rotation, while Austin Wells was locked in the trunk of a car for four months, while shortstop was an open question until the season’s final few weeks. It should be kind of remarkable that they were even in the dance in the first place?

But the AL was so bad, the table so uncompetitive, that the Yankees didn’t really outrun the other guy being chased by the bear. There was no bear at all. The team wasn’t good enough to chase down the Rays, dooming themselves to an additional two playoff games while the Rays got to rest, prepare, and welcome the Yankees to the Trop for the start of the series. The same offense we’d seen sleepwalk through the year for weeks at a time showed themselves, they lost, and I don’t really care.

Supposedly at the staff level the organization is starting to pick at itself like an under-stimulated pet bird. This annual tradition of “just be good enough to make it before 26 people who should be among the best in the world at what they do collectively forget what their jobs are” might finally be sinking in. At the top level though we’ll be told not to worry, There is A Plan, these guys are having good at bats actually, it’s right in front of us.

Congratulations to the New York Yankees. You’ve managed to accomplish something my government and AI companies haven’t. Sure, man, whatever you say, I shrug my shoulders and I walk down the street.
