title: Winners and losers from F1's wet Singapore GP sprint race
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
But that still demanded cool heads of the 22 drivers - some of whom were more successful at keeping cool than others.

Here's our pick of winners and losers from the sixth and final sprint race of the 2026 Formula 1 season.

“I just misjudged it,” George Russell said of his early race-ending Singapore crash.

Even if this is likely to make no difference to his ever-dwindling title hopes, Russell is in a position where, for his own sake, he needs to end the year on a high.

Grabbing the lead from Verstappen at the start in the sprint looked like the perfect way to do that before a grid penalty hobbles the rest of his weekend.

But the heavy crash - which he put down to having more power than expected from the battery exiting the final corner and then touching the white line as he ran a little wide - put paid to that in a very painful way.

“It's a very, very silly mistake,” he said. “Overly confident. Think it's my first crash of the year. It's annoying to happen from that position.”

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (4th)

This was a quintessential ‘when it’s your year, it’s your year’ kind of day for Kimi Antonelli.

He did nothing remarkable - which in itself is good because evidently these were conditions it was easy to trip up in - and yet took another little step towards his world championship.

His chief title ‘rival’ Russell crashed out of a winning position on the first lap. Then, at the very end, two cars ahead of him were removed by a needless collision.

Apart from keeping the car on the road this is the easiest progress Antonelli will make all season - and it almost ended in an unlikely sprint podium, such was Leclerc’s trouble by the end of the race.

Loser: McLaren (8th & 14th)

A frustrating but solid race turned into a needlessly destructive one for McLaren thanks to Lando Norris’s over-ambitious final lap move.

Sending it down the inside of Turn 5 in the wet is borderline desperate at the best of times, let alone against your team-mate.

McLaren chiefs must have been holding their breath when it happened but ultimately, while gutted, surely not surprised that it caused a synchronised pirouette from the pair, ending Oscar Piastri’s race in the process.

It was always likely to end badly and it could yet get worse if Norris cops a penalty for it that loses him eighth place, and with it the measly point McLaren still got as a weak silver lining.

Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)

Would Verstappen have had anything to come back at Russell with? We'll never know - though you could infer that Verstappen might've found it difficult considering his assertion post-race that "I think we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass".

That's all academic. Verstappen never looked under threat from behind, and his drive to victory had an air of cruise control to it - at a track, too, where Verstappen can struggle to reach his peak level of performance.

Yet more evidence that the four-time champion is the form driver right now.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (DNF)

It's hard to judge Hadjar too harshly considering he managed only two laps before parking up with a power issue.

But he did lose two places at the start, if we're being ultra-critical.

And of course, there's no escaping the fact this was a DNF in a race won by the sister car.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (2nd)

Lewis Hamilton did the hard work for his sprint race in the opening few seconds, leaping forward past his team-mate and the two McLarens.

Considering he seemed to have the best pace of anyone besides Verstappen in this race, that was critical. Getting stuck on a track where it looked almost impossible to overtake in these conditions - barring bigger pace swings in the midfield - would have made Hamilton’s sprint look a lot more average.

He couldn't quite match Verstappen in the middle of the race but started to whittle away at the lead again late on and was much, much better managing his tyres than team-mate Leclerc seemed to be as the track dried.

Winner: Liam Lawson (5th)

If you can keep your head when all around you are losing theirs...

OK, the Singapore sprint wasn't the most difficult to navigate in reality, but there was still plenty of reward to be reaped from keeping it neat and tidy.

This was another exemplary drive from Lawson, who in repeating his best-of-the-rest trick from qualifying also stood to gain from any incidents up ahead. (Hello, McLaren.)

It's this sort of drive that means the direction of travel is only going one way in the fight for fifth in the constructors' championship between Racing Bulls and Alpine right now.

Loser: Arvid Lindblad (13th)

Compare Lawson's serene run to fifth with Racing Bulls team-mate Lindblad's travails.

Lindblad was perplexed after the race by his spin under the safety car - "it was a bit confusing at the time because it was pretty gentle on power, then just suddenly lost it" - but was a little loose in his description of events that "then I tried to just get it back round", as he in fact had spent multiple seconds driving the car backwards while trying to loop around at Turn 5.

No surprise then that that caught the attention of race control.

And even if he escapes penalty, this was a last-on-the-road finish in the same car that finished well up the road in fifth. There's no question, considering the attrition, that points were up for grabs.

Loser: Cadillac (DNF & DNF)

Two cars. Two collisions. One unproductive race.

The Sergio Perez-Lance Stroll clash looked like as clear a case of racing incident as you'll find, so there's little blame to be apportioned to the Cadillac driver there.

Valtteri Bottas doesn't get such an easy ride. What initially looked like a lazy slide from Alex Albon into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto was actually the result of Bottas getting into the back of the Williams. All this before the race had restarted, too.

The "rubber band" effect was partly to blame - Bottas said "the two cars ahead of me came to full stop and I just didn't have time to react" - but he did ultimately trigger contact.

So much for this being the sort of weekend, and track, that can play into Cadillac's hands...

Winner: Ollie Bearman (6th)

Ollie Bearman was absolutely thrilled with his work in the sprint, even though he acknowledged his seven-place rise was bolstered by others screwing up.

Irrespective of the Russell shunt and McLaren collision, though, Bearman was a man on the move here. He toughed it out nicely to get ahead of Pierre Gasly once the race resumed post-safety car, and that was critical for consolidating a points finish.

Bearman was on course to grab eighth irrespective of what happened on the final lap - so the bump up to sixth merely boosted the Haas driver rather than flattered his efforts completely.

title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review. Experts are alarmed
author: Tom Perkins
text:
Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review.

The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb).

But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage .

The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing.

The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “ promises kept ” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken , injure or kill people.

But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception.

Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science.

“The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues.

“I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added.

The FDA did not respond to a request for comment.

The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”.

Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts.

Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”.

Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity.

Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical.

“They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.”

The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats.

Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample.

Perchlorate reduces the thyroid gland’s ability to absorb iodine, which is a raw material needed to produce the hormone T4, an essential component of proper brain development . Very low levels of perchlorate exposure are linked to lower T4 production, and lower IQ scores for children.

Still, six months after it published its data, the FDA reapproved perchlorate for use in super sacks. Advocates say the agency used flawed science and manipulated the data. The FDA wrote that there was no meaningful increase in perchlorate across all the 250 foods it measured. But critics countered that the problem was not in all the food – the problem was in kids’ cereal.

The FDA largely ignored the cereal findings, and mostly does not consider endocrine system harms when developing regulations, said Tom Neltner, a former scientist with the EDF who is now director of the Unleaded Kids non-profit. He helped lead litigation over perchlorate, which was ultimately dismissed.

“They put their blinders on and approved the exemption based on data that never considered the harms posed by endocrine disruptors,” Neltner said.…

title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean
author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
text:
Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality

They were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In the Peterloo massacre of 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.

A study by Global Threads , a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – as Robert Wedderburn , a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.

As well as looking at Wedderburn’s story , Global Threads’ research looks at the life of Hugh Hornby Birley, the yeomanry commander who led the fatal charge on the crowd at Peterloo. It found Birley’s family fortune was intimately linked with transatlantic enslavement.

Meanwhile, the story of Sir George Philips , also examined in the project, reflects the contradictions of 19th-century liberal politics. While Philips helped fund the Manchester Guardian as a liberal reaction to Peterloo, he was personally invested in the exploitation of enslaved Africans in the Caribbean, as owner of the Success plantation in Hanover, Jamaica.

Birley and Philips were members of the Portico Library , Manchester’s historic members’ library. In the 19th century it was a centre of information exchange for Manchester’s business elite, helping ensure their place at the apex of global capitalism. The Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico, which stands a few yards from where the Peterloo massacre took place.

Introducing the study, Global Threads said: “Drawing together just three of the thousands of threads connecting Peterloo with Africa and the Americas, we can see how the leaders of each wing of Manchester’s elite – Hugh Hornby Birley and Sir George Philips – owed their positions and power to their family and business activities drawing on colonialism and slavery.

“They actively described the system they had created as a transatlantic one. It was not just profit that connected Peterloo … Birley and his reactionary colleagues brought colonial-style coercion more akin to the putting down of uprisings of enslaved people, working people themselves were connected to transatlantic people and places, and slavery hung like a spectre over the Mancunian struggles for justice and equality.”

On 16 August 1819, 60,000 people converged in the centre of Manchester to campaign for political representation. Conditions for those workers were better than those endured by the trafficked and enslaved African workers at the other end of the transatlantic commodity boom, who were classed as property. But Britain’s working class were disenfranchised. Only 10% of men in the country could vote, and while landowners were enriched by the tariffs placed on foreign grain by the Corn Laws, workers could barely afford bread.

The protest at St Peter’s Field ended in tragedy when the yeomanry – a militia of Tory businessmen – charged the crowd. In the aftermath, the authorities blamed protesters. But Wedderburn, a Jamaican-born Unitarian preacher, was quick to challenge the official narrative.

In September 1819, at a meeting at his Soho chapel, he described Peterloo as “an act of murder … committed by the magistrates and yeoman”. In his preaching and writings, Wedderburn had long argued Africans and English labourers were being denied by the same forces.

The backstory of Birley shows how. Ella Sinclair, writing for Global Threads, found Birley’s family’s business financially benefited from the estate of Daniel Backhouse, an enslaver who funded and profited from 103 voyages that set out from Liverpool between 1773 and 1807, trafficking more than 27,000 Africans.

In the late 18th century, three of those voyages exported people to St Lucia, where Backhouse’s company funded and profited from the Rabot sugar estate. Early 19th-century records reveal that workers there included families trafficked from Guinea and Cape Verde.

After the emancipation of enslaved Africans in the British empire in the 1830s, the Birley family supported the enslaving US confederacy, which was integral to their cotton interests. Birley was closely involved with the development of Manchester institutions, including “the Liverpool and Manchester Railway – designed to more easily transport slave-produced cotton”, Sinclair found.

Wedderburn’s family was also embedded in the plantation economy. His uncle, John Wedderburn, owned the Blackheath, Blackness, Bluecastle and Glen Islay plantations in Westmoreland, Jamaica. Workers on those plantations included people trafficked from Old Calabar, in modern-day Nigeria, to Montego Bay in 1773, on a ship carrying textiles woven in Manchester.

Robert Wedderburn’s mother was an enslaved woman called Rosanne, while his father was the plantation owner who raped her. Raised in Jamaica by his African grandmother, Talky Amee, Wedderburn served in the Royal Navy and sailed to London, settling in multicultural St Giles and became a leading radical.

Global Threads found that the Dreadnought, the ship that trafficked some enslaved workers to Wedderburn plantations, had also trafficked workers to Success, the plantation later owned by Philips.

At the time of Peterloo, Wedderburn was in prison, accused of inciting slaves to kill their masters. He believed in armed struggle against enslavement across the Caribbean, and that a revolution had begun at Peterloo.…

title: Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
author: Agence France-Presse
text:
Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes

A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.

The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.

The candidate from the leftwing Ahora Nación party won 229 out of a total of 663 votes in elections on 4 October, according to the national office of electoral processes.

His closest rival, the far-right candidate Gaspar Osorio, received 204 votes.

Flores, who works in freight transportation, had belonged to Popular Force, the party of Peru’s rightwing president, Keiko Fujimori, until 2025, according to electoral authorities.

Despite the name being associated with Germany’s Nazi leader Adolf Hitler, several candidates with the name have won elections in Peru.

In 2021, the doctor Hitler Saavedra Casternoque was elected to parliament for the centrist party Somos Peru.

In 2018, Hitler Alba Sánchez was voted in as mayor of the Andean district of Yungar, saying during his campaign that he was “the good Hitler”.

You might already know about the HTX Studio YouTube channel, but if you don’t, trust me , you need to check it out. It’s a team of makers and creators from China who are making some of the most innovative tech videos I’ve seen in years. title: ‘People Are Dying’: Riders Delay Il Lombardia in Rare Public Protest Over Safety
author: ahood
text:
Remco Evenepoel, shown here with world champion Brandon McNulty, spoke out on behalf of the peloton over rider safety. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

The riders have had enough, and the bunch delayed Il Lombardia for five minutes Saturday morning to demand safer roads after another ugly week of vehicles getting onto race courses .

World champion Brandon McNulty and European champion Remco Evenepoel stood at the front as the peloton held up the season’s final monument to demand rider safety .

Evenepoel grabbed the microphone and spoke for the riders in a rare public showing of solidarity.

“In the name of the whole bunch and not only for the guys that are here but for everybody pro cycling, we want to make this statement because there’s too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race,” Evenepoel said.

“Unfortunately, we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us,” he said. “We want to make this statement to just show to the whole world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured and are literally dying while doing what we like the most.”

The riders and the CPA also issued a joint statement asking the UCI and race organizers to take responsibility and tighten course security ( see statement below ).

Frustration has been bubbling behind the scenes ever since 19-year-old Finlay Tarling was killed following a collision with a vehicle that entered the Volta a Portugal course in August.

Michael Tarling, the father of Finlay, took to X to support the solidarity among the riders.

“We are so thankful, moved and proud of Fin’s fellow cyclists today for making a stand at the Tour of Lombardy,” he wrote. “Things need to change and no other family should ever receive the phone call we received on 14th Aug. We sincerely hope the UCI are listening and changes will be made.”

‼️ La protesta del pelotón, encabezada por Remco Evenepoel, antes del inicio de #IlLombardia ⚠️ El movimiento llega tras los últimos incidentes con vehículos de carrera estas semanas #LaCasadelCiclismo pic.twitter.com/OgEwYGlIwq

Saturday’s protest comes on the heels of high-profile vehicle incidents at both Coppa Bernocchi and Tre Valli Varesine this week in Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi, a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route from a side street and drove behind the breakaway before stopping.

A day later, a police motorbike traveling against the direction of racing collided with Tom Pidcock’s Pinarello-Q36.5 teammates Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubí at Tre Valli Varesine.

Gloag abandoned and required stitches to his knee , while Camprubí continued and later complained that “nothing changes.”

Heavy crashes have marked racing this week in Italy as well .

The latest incidents add to a grim toll the past few years. Gino Mäder died after crashing at the 2023 Tour de Suisse, André Drege died while descending at the Tour of Austria in 2024, and junior racer Muriel Furrer died following a crash at the 2024 UCI Road World Championships.

“This is why we want to stand for five minutes more, to make our statement towards organizations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling and accepting the fact that people are dying,” Evenepoel said.

The UCI has introduced new safety measures , including better barriers and signage, but riders want faster action and stronger protection on race roads.

“We want to pay our tribute and respect to everybody that was already involved in the incidents,” he said.

After the protest, the race started without further incident.

There was no immediate response from the UCI.

As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to.

This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer.

Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

We are calling for the help of the UCI for race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one.

We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones.

title: Verstappen urges Red Bull to fix race starts problem
Squeezy olive oil bottles, Meghan’s pot filler tap and the rise of ‘cheffy’ kit in home kitchens
author: Ellie Violet Bramley
text:
Social media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buying

T he Duchess of Sussex is no ordinary home cook, but when Meghan appeared on Instagram this week at a hob presided over by a special pot filler tap , it spoke to a shift in the everyday kitchen – the rise of “cheffy” kit.

While the pot filler is now most often found in luxury residential kitchens, it was reportedly invented in the early 20th century as a functional fixture for commercial kitchens. It joins a wealth of other restaurant equipment to have infiltrated our homes, from squeezy olive oil bottles to stainless steel mixing bowl sets.

At Sous Chef, a UK-based independent speciality food brand, sales of chef presses are up 26%, while sales of chef’s trays are booming, according to Holly Thomson, the company’s food editor.

For Ella Risbridger, author of The Kitchen Book: Good Food for Every Day : “It’s an amazing thing, the blurring of lines between restaurant and home kitchens.” A byproduct of the increasing visibility we have of professional chefs at work, whether via open kitchens in restaurants or “chefluencers” on social media, the utilitarianism and gadgets of restaurant kitchens are increasingly aspirational. This week, in a home tour with Architectural Digest, Julianne Moore showed off her Ikea industrial shelves.

“People now can see what is happening in professional kitchens,” says Risbridger, “and likely, if they are watching The Bear or a lot of cheffy Instagrams, the algorithm knows that and knows what you might, might, want to buy for yourself.” From the white T-shirt to the Japanese Hasegawa chopping board , people want to channel Carmy and Syd as they make dinner midweek.

Thomson suspects it might have something to do with the economic climate – people are thinking: “‘I’m not going to spend 90 quid on a meal, but I might invest in these products that are going to help me take eating at home a bit more seriously.’” According to James Lawless, a spokesperson at David Mellor, this shift links back to the pandemic, which “reignited interest in home cooking”.

“Professional chefs’ equipment may have specialist functions, but it isn’t special,” says Lawless. “They are first and foremost tools to perform a particular function.”

For Thomson, they are “an extra piece of kit that adds a bit of ease, finesse, or streamlines the process”. Coming from a professional kitchen, where “you don’t have anything that takes up space that isn’t fully useful, used every day and has multiple purposes,” they’d have to be.

Of course, one person’s useful can be another’s waste of space. In the case of the pot filler tap, in an ordinary small kitchen that might be unnecessary, but, according to Helen Parker, the creative director of deVOL Kitchens, it “has become the must-have addition to a larger kitchen”.

Sometimes, you don’t know what you don’t know. As Thomson says of the squeezy olive oil bottle, which, at a few quid, is proof that this isn’t all about expensive equipment: “Precision squirting is just so useful, and once you’ve done it once, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is so much better than glugging oil out of a bottle.’”

For Risbridger, “the trick is that it’s nice to buy something fancy for a hobby – it’s often a shortcut to taking yourself more seriously … you can now access a reasonably cheap version of something professionals use, and that makes you feel more like a professional. Which increases confidence. Which makes the thing you make better, whether or not you could have achieved it without the gadget.”

title: Greens must avoid ‘capture by extremists and racists’, says party MP
author: Geneva Abdul
text:
Ellie Chowns says vote for ‘Zionism is racism’ policy by 0.4% of members shows party processes are not working

A Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists” amid the continuing fallout from the “Zionism is racism” vote.

The party faces a political maelstrom over its policy decision last week to treat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, as any other form of racism, and to back a single Palestinian state over a two-state solution. The motion was passed at the annual party conference with just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.

Ellie Chowns, the party leader in the House of Commons, said the ability to pass such a “significant and damaging policy” in that way made it clear the party’s structures and policymaking processes were not working.

“I don’t think that policy, ‘Zionism is racism’, represents the large majority of Green party members, nor of people in the country,” Chowns told BBC’s Radio 4 Today Programme on Saturday.

“We don’t want to be in debates about the meaning of contested terms, we want to be united and focusing in contesting and criticising the horrific actions of the Israeli government,” said Chowns, who lost a co-leadership run against Zack Polanski in 2025.

The debate over whether the Greens’ decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly comes hours after the party’s leader for England and Wales was defeated by Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection .

Polanksi, who received just under 33% of the vote on Friday, insisted he intended to remain as Green leader, despite calls to stand down , including from the chair of the Jewish Greens. The party normally holds leadership elections every two years, meaning the next election would be in the summer of 2027.

Chowns said Polanksi’s “clear” lack of leadership over the Zionisim motion was “disappointing”, but that he had an opportunity to unite the party, having recognised the flaws in the motion.

Tensions were heightened between the UK and Israel after the Labour government imposed sanctions on illegal settlements in occupied Palestine, and Israel retaliated by trying to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.

Research carried out before the motion was passed found that Jewish people who vote for the Greens felt their attachment to Israel had weakened , even as the percentage of British Jews who identified as Zionist rose more broadly between 2022 and 2025.

When asked about extremism and racism within the party – not only in relation to the motion but comments made by the deputy leader, Mothin Ali, after the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 in which he called for an end to “white supremacist European settler colonialism” – Chowns stressed the importance of the party’s internal processes.

“I don’t know if there are extremists and racists in my party but I want to make sure that my party isn’t vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, I want to make sure my party’s policies represent the views of the majority of members of the Green party who absolutely are not that sort of person at all,” she said.

“Of course its legitimate to have difference of opinions including on many of the matters that this motion covers,” she added.

Polanski has been accused of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate and the vote at the conference to instead campaign in the byelection, and for giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.

In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.

On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein , the chair of the Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”

However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.

title: Premier League today: How to watch Manchester United v Spurs, TV channels & live stream

How will Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options

The sense of desperation will be strong as Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur arrive at Old Trafford with both teams in bad need of a win to change the narrative around their disappointing seasons so far.

Anything less than three points would further increase the pressure on Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi , both of whom are fighting to prove they are the right people for their respective jobs. Saturday’s match could be pivotal.

Spurs can take encouragement from the fact they have won four of their last six encounters with United in all competitions dating back to September 2024. Less positive is their run of four blanks in the five league matches they have played so far this season.

Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.

United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports Main Event

Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur have suffered many of the same problems to start the season. Both teams have conceded far too many goals and struggled for any sort of defensive foundation. The former have yet to keep a single clean sheet in five league games while the latter have kept just two.

In midfield, Carrick and De Zerbi struggling for the right balance. Manchester United and Spurs both bought expensive new midfielders in the summer transfer window who have yet to settle into their new surroundings.

Things haven’t been much better in the attacking third where Spurs have scored in just one of their five league games. For Manchester United, the likes of Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Bryan Mbeumo have yet to find top form. This match could be a catalyst, but it’s not clear for whom.

title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
text:
Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll

Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.

Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.

The Cockroach movement , as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi ‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.

Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi . More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.

On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”

Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.

Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.

Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge.

In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.

Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.

In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.

Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.

Buses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.

Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.

After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”

Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”

Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.

“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”…

title: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
author: Jacek Krywko
text:
For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”

In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.

Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.

title: Tourism expansion v turtle nests: the dispute dividing communities in one Tobago resort
author: Jewel Fraser in Rocky Point, Tobago
text:
Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat

V isitors to Rocky Point in south-west Tobago are drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest.

But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best.

As elsewhere in the Caribbean, the need for economic growth has led to growing interest in tourism development. Rene Seepersadsingh, the first vice-president of the Tobago Hotel and Tourism Association , says: “Tobago is very focused on attracting private partnership investment because our tourism product is now in that evolution stage, where we’re looking to upgrade the offering that we have.

“There are great opportunities for participation and development within the sector,” he adds.

With that goal in mind, the 12 hectares (30 acres) of Rocky Point became the subject of a request for expressions of interest in 2021 from the government agency Eteck , which manages and develops economic zones.

Eteck invited proposals from qualified firms to design and manage a premier hotel and property development on the site. Superior Hotels, a locally owned company, ultimately won. It received a 99-year lease to develop a $500m (£378m), 200-room property on the site, which also includes plans for a number of privately owned villas.

Since then, the project has sparked a struggle that has been going on for the past four years, led by environmentalists, Tobagonians and others who believe the development will ruin Rocky Point.

Duane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation – one of several entities that submitted an expression of interest to Eteck – is now advocating for increased accountability. A former hotel manager, he is an avid surfer at Back Bay and owns tourism-related businesses in Tobago.

“Our focus is to make sure that whatever is done on that site is done in an environmentally sound way, in a way that preserves it for Tobago and for future generations,” he says.

He says he and his associates replied to the expression of interest with a proposal for a small eco-resort featuring nature trails, turtle watching and a wax museum showcasing Amerindian artefacts discovered at Rocky Point. He also highlighted the remains of Fort Monck, a distinctive fort with well-preserved masonry.

Kenny says the winning project’s initial design raised concerns about it seemingly ignoring many archaeological and ecological features at Rocky Point, and that the subsequent amendments still do not adequately address many of the issues raised.

“The amount of concrete development on this site, at least in the current model, makes us worry that the impact on the environment will be significant,” he says, adding that in his view a 200-room hotel has little chance of success in Tobago, where most large hotels struggle to achieve sustainable occupancy levels.

Michelle Cazabon-Mannette, an environmental biologist and director at the NGO SpeSeas , says more than 100 people submitted written objections to the Environmental Management Authority (EMA) as part of the environmental impact assessment, which the project needs to obtain a certificate of environmental clearance (CEC). She says that after widespread objections at town hall meetings and in written submissions, the project holder made only minor design adjustments.

After the adjustments, the EMA granted Superior Hotels a CEC , with about 20 pages of mitigation measures attached that the project must follow.

Kirkland Brathwaite, principal at Katalyst Solutions, an environmental and project management firm, says a CEC often includes several environmental impact mitigation measures, adding that a quality assurance project plan is mandatory to ensure proper monitoring.

Cazabon-Mannette says the mitigation measures listed in the CEC are insufficient, though she acknowledges that “the project designs provided – on which the CEC is based – were conceptual and (Superior Hotels) made it clear these were not final designs”.

Whatever form the final designs take, Cazabon-Mannette and Kenny say a 200-room hotel and numerous villas will probably mean removing many of the trees on Rocky Point. “A major concern is having an appropriate scale of development that would minimise the footprint in terms of the coastal vegetation that would need to be cleared,” Cazabon-Mannette says.

She adds that the trees provide shade and help protect the beach from coastal erosion, and their removal would harm one of Tobago’s most important turtle nesting sites. “At Back Bay, the shade keeps the sand cool,” she says, making it a choice for hawksbill turtles and leatherback turtles laying their eggs.

Cazabon-Mannette says that sediment runoff from development could also threaten the unique coral reef that makes it a surfer’s paradise. The developer has promised to set up silt fences during construction to control sediment runoff, but “these things fail all the time”, Kenny says.

When questioned about the concerns of environmentalists, John Aboud, chairman of Superior Hotels T&T, replied to the Guardian by forwarding the CEC, without further comment.

While the EMA approval has been issued, final approvals from Tobago’s Town and Country Planning Division and the assembly, its legislative body, remain under review.…

title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales
author: Joanna Partridge in Cardigan
text:
In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan

Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales.

Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely.

When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere.

Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople.

Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16.

“I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape.

In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer.

When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”.

As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival , held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan.

Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim.

The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week.

The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs.

“The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.”

Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way.

Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge.

Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders.

Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company.

One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan.

He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies.

“We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.”

The family has committed to keeping the manufacturing in Cardigan, although von Loeper adds that the factory’s west Wales location creates logistical challenges when moving finished garments or bringing in photographers and models for photoshoots.

He adds: “The thing that attracted all of us to Hiut was the purpose of making jeans again, and not just for the sake of making jeans, but to have the jobs, to have to craft, to have skills remain here.”

Some high-profile visitors have tried out the craft. A framed photo and letter from Kensington palace hangs on the factory wall, commemorating the March visit of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, where she had a go on a sewing machine.

Walking past huge rolls of fabric from some of the most prestigious denim mills in the world – in Japan, Italy and Turkey – von Loeper says he faced a big decision shortly after taking over running the company. A key Japanese denim supplier warned Hiut and other long-term customers that operational pressures meant it was about to close its order books until 2027.…

title: ‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staff
author: Michael Sainato
text:
Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale

U nion officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints.

“People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth.

TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”.

Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs.

“People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.”

“Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.”

Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturers recommend sitting while operating the machines.

Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations.

Following the policy change, TSA workers were also required to sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union.

“They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones.

He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US.

Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents.

US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy.

“A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.”

AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees, launched a letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”.

Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented.

“Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.”

The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facing possible pay freezes and significant increases to their health insurance premium costs.

Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judge ruling in January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction.

TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year.

The Trump administration has also been expanding privatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airport abandoned its plan to join the program.

TSA did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the policy change and union’s criticisms of the policy and morale pledge. TSA still requires a chair must be available upon request for travelers.

“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News on the policy change, but did not cite why the agency did not negotiate the change with the union.

“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”

title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily
author: Lorenzo Tondo in Palermo
text:
Marsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from Mediterranean

Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.

A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.

Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.

A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.

In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.

The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.

According to experts , record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.
