title: Three winners and three losers from Knicks’ first two preseason games
author: Kento Kato
text:
The Knicks are back to playing basketball and are less than two weeks away from opening night. They’ve started 0-2, which nobody really cares about, but we’ve also now seen enough minutes from the exhibition matches to get a glimpse of who the winners and losers have been in the early portion of the preseason.

Winner: Jalen Brunson and his wrist

Should anyone have really doubted or even been remotely worried about Brunson’s offseason wrist surgery? No, the captain has repeatedly been the definition of reliable. So it was ridiculous to ever think that Brunson wouldn’t be prepared or would look off coming off of his injury. But fans are unreasonable. And also, he is a 30 year-old who had an operation on his shooting hand.

Fortunately for Knicks fans, though, he’s looked as good as any other Knicks. His three-point shot was off against the Wizards as he went just 1-for-6. But Brunson looks like he’s in midseason form. He’s taking his usual shots, which include, but aren’t limited to, driving layups, floaters, mid-range fadeaways, and pull-up threes, and he’s looked comfortable and confident in doing so. Defensively, he’s started the preseason giving good effort, and he’s already drawn multiple charges as well. Brunson and his wrist seem to be doing just fine.

Loser: Pacome Dadiet and his trade value

Coming into training camp and preseason, there couldn’t have been many expectations for Dadiet. He’s now had two full seasons of pretty much being non-existent. His Summer League left a lot to be desired. And he played worse than most fans could’ve imagined during the World Cup qualifiers for the Ivory Coast team. Yet even after all that, he’s found a way to disappoint so far in preseason. In the preseason opener, the team was clearly trying to give him an opportunity to either increase his trade value or at least win some spot minutes, and he failed to do that. And he wasn’t much better in game two against the Wizards.

It’s only been two games, but they’ve both been a failure for Dadiet. He’s scored just nine total points in 30 minutes of play and is shooting just 28.6% from the field without standing out as a playmaker, rebounder, or defender. Dadiet’s path to being a rotation player in New York was pretty thin to begin with. But whatever opportunity he had to at least help the team out by increasing his trade value may be slipping away now too.

Shamet is coming off of two straight training camps where his job wasn’t even guaranteed. He’s battled back from injuries and has consistently displayed a perfect balance of selflessness and staying ready. That led to him becoming an integral part of the Knicks’ rotation last year. And he was rewarded with a very nice four-year, $24 million contract. Shamet rewarded the Knicks and their loyalty by reportedly turning down offers from other contenders.

Now back with the same team for the third straight year-something he’s never done before in his career-the journeyman looks comfortable and confident. He looks poised to not just continue what he’s done but build upon it and has gotten off to an extremely hot start in preseason. He’s averaging 11.5PPG in just 13.5MPG and is shooting an extremely hot 53.3% from the field and 50% from three.

The talk around McBride for much of the offseason has been about what the Knicks could get in a trade for him. And after the offensive struggles he went through in the Finals, there are some fans who may have forgotten just how good and valuable the reserve guard is. He’s still one of the best bench perimeter defenders in the league, and that, combined with his much improved three-point shooting, makes him so pivotal to what Mike Brown and the Knicks want to do. And nobody should be overly concerned about what he does or doesn’t do in the preseason.

That being said, he’s currently struggling mightily offensively. McBride has so far averaged just 3PPG on 18.2% shooting from the field and 11.1% shooting from three. There were some expectations that he’d showcase a little more after a full offseason to work on some of his weaknesses that got exposed against the Spurs. And fans were excited to see him fully healthy after he revealed that he was still hurt throughout the postseason run. He should be fine eventually, but it’s been a rough go for McBride so far.

Many fans had different reactions when Drummond signed with the Knicks this past summer. Some were excited, some were indifferent, and some were disappointed. New York still has a very long season ahead of them, and that should come with opportunities to upgrade at this position one way or another. And during said long season, Drummond will inevitably go through ups and downs. But so far, the veteran center has looked solid.

His pick-and-roll defense, something many were concerned about, has actually looked good. He’s been very active with his hands, and his defense there, especially when paired up with the also active Jose Alvarado, could be a fun tandem. Drummond’s finishing ability is concerning due to his lack of explosiveness. But his surprisingly solid defense, along with his elite-as-advertised rebounding, has been fun to watch.

Losers: Drew Eubanks, Ochai Agbaji, and Tony Bradley

Bruce Brown Jr. was looked at as one of the favorites to win the Knicks’ last roster spot given the team’s previous interest in him. Other than that, there really wasn’t a consensus. Some wanted James Wiseman for his potential. Others wanted Eubanks for his defense, passing, and experience. Others wanted Agbaji for… not really sure why.

Two games into preseason, it looks clear who Brown and the Knicks have the most interest in. Brown, Wiseman, and Jaden Akins are the only three of the training camp invitees to play in both games. On Thursday night against the Wizards, Eubanks, Agbaji, and Bradley were DNPs. Now, this may just be the way they are splitting up the minutes, and maybe those guys see minutes over Brown and Wiseman when they play the Timberwolves on Monday. Brown, although not overly impressive, has looked solid. And Wiseman, especially against the 76ers, looked good. Neither is locked in to make the roster just yet. But it seems like they are a head above Eubanks, Agbaji, and Bradley.

title: The director of Fjord takes the ‘risky position’ of moderator
author: May Jeong
text:
With his new film about a Romanian family’s life in Norway, Cristian Mungiu wants you to consider the limits of your tolerance﻿

With his new film about a Romanian family’s life in Norway, Cristian Mungiu wants you to consider the limits of your tolerance﻿

Cristian Mungiu’s sixth feature, Fjord , concerns a family on trial. They seem like good people, God-fearing. They’ve just moved from Romania to a small hamlet nestled in the fjords of rural Norway. There is Mamma (Renate Reinsve), Tata (a bald and bespectacled Sebastian Stan), and their passel of children. They are an openly religious and proselytizing family. The parents, unfashionably, believe in punitive consequences to actions. They would never be accused of gentle parenting. All ought to be well, only Norway in 2026 is extravagantly suspicious of the devout — their famous tolerance reserved for the secular.

Fjord starts quietly and builds subtly. We are with the family as they are introduced to their places of learning, employment, and worship. A second, Norwegian, family serves as their foil. Sort of. Questions arise, about what counts as discipline, what as punishment. To those wanting answers, objective analysis, which is to say a kind of measured purity, Mungiu says, come down to the mud with us! In the morally complex world of the movie, nothing is spared — a piano chord, a passing remark, hems of clothes — all are cast in a different light. We are all the more enriched for it.

The Verge spoke with Mungiu, who is himself Romanian, about how his early tenure in journalism informs his writing, what it was like living under Nicolae Ceaușescu’s dictatorial reign, Marxist literary theory, and the challenges and pleasures of thinking for oneself.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

I’d like to start with you at Cannes, where you said the question that Fjord raises is: Are there good minorities and bad minorities? I wonder if this question has changed for you since.

Not so much. I think that as much as we need to understand that there are good values in society, like tolerance for all the other minorities and inclusion of those who are different than us, we should always focus on this idea that sometimes even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well. If not, what makes us believe that we have a more liberal, progressive view on the world?

Of course, there is a limit. We all need to condemn violence, and we all need to be on the same side of helping people out.

But whenever we talk about, for example, religious beliefs, even if we are people who don’t share such beliefs, it’s good to be tolerant with them, if they want to share different views. You need to let them be.

“Even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well.”

There are so many people next to us who share a lot of irrational beliefs, from reading the horoscope to believing in alternative medicine. We let them be. Why would we condemn people for being religious? It’s good to try to convince them that actually it’s good to see that your beliefs are based on something rational, because eventually, we all influence the lives of others, and it’s good to make choices based on rational things. But you need to advance little by little, step by step. I don’t believe in this way of imposing views on others and making rules for others to change what they think. If you do that, you will only radicalize people.

You said you kept chancing upon articles about immigrant families in Nordic countries. Is reading the news part of your practice? Otherwise, where have your ideas come from?

I read a lot of news every day, and I keep a lot of these articles in special folders under different themes. And it took years before I decided to make a film based on the ideas in these articles, because in the beginning they are very spectacular. They are just informing us about something spectacular that has happened. While for me, the film should be something deeper, more profound, in the sense that I’m trying to figure out why those things have happened and what do they tell us about the world around us?

I try to avoid the sensational part of it and to try to dig down, and to understand what is it that it could tell you about your own life, and this is what I did for the original story as well. I needed some eight years from the moment when I read about it to the moment when I decided to make a film out of it.

Tell me more about your excavation process. Can you walk us through what is actually happening in those eight years? And specifically, can you tell us about the moment in the process when you go from research to fiction? What does that leap look like, or maybe it’s seamless?

It’s fair to say that I haven’t used all these 10 years to investigate. But I was aware all the time that this exists. For example, I decided to talk to this family who was involved in the most prominent case, in the most spoken-about case, from three years ago. I talked to them. I talked to their children. I went to Norway. I met their relatives. I went to see the house where everything happened. I took advantage in that moment to investigate more, and I met everybody that I could who was involved in that case. And people who were willing to talk to me. I talked to lawyers. I talked to all the press that covered the case. I talked to the translator they were having when talking to the police. I talked to the Barnevernet [Norwegian child welfare agency]. I talked to the NGOs who were involved a lot in such cases. Later on, I was a witness to the trials they were having on children issues. So I did my best to find all the points of view of people involved, not only in that case but in other cases.…

title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
author: Abigail Bassett
text:
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.

Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.

I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.

The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.

The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.

People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights

Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.

Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”

Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.

Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”

Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.

“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.

For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.…

title: Bauke Mollema, Pello Bilbao and other retiring riders receive guard of honour send-off at Il Lombardia
author: Matilda Price
text:
The retiring riders for whom Il Lombardia will be their final race received a warm send-off and a guard of honour from the peloton at the start of the Italian Monument in Bergamo on Saturday morning.

Multiple riders are closing the curtain on their careers in Italy this Saturday, including former winner Bauke Mollema (Lidl-Trek), plus Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious), Rudy Molard (Groupama-FDJ United), Odd Christian Eiking (Unibet Rose Rockets) and Ion Izagirre (Cofidis).

At the start, the retirees were presented with a guard of honour from their peloton colleagues, who lined the road with their bikes in the air to wave off the departing riders.

Mollema, who won this race in 2019 and has the most starts in the current peloton with a whopping 17, was also presented with a medal and framed plaque on stage during the team sign-on to commemorate the last race of his career.

This comes alongside a special Netherlands-themed paint job on his Trek bike for his final race.

"There's quite a lot going through my mind today, it's a special day, ending my career here in Lombardia, in a race that I won and that has given me a lot," the Dutchman told at the start.

"It's been a long journey, almost 20 years in professional cycling, and today is the last day, in a race I love. I've always loved to race in Italy, so I hope to enjoy it a bit, but it will also be a lot of suffering."

title: Verstappen wins delayed Singapore sprint, Russell crashes from lead
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Max Verstappen won an attritional Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix sprint race bookended by initial race leader George Russell crashing out and the two McLarens colliding.

After a delayed start due to heavy rain in the build-up to the sprint, Russell jumped Verstappen into the first corner - but his lead barely lasted a full lap.

The Mercedes driver, for whom a win might have barely kept alive his faint title hopes, spun exiting the final corner and crashed into the pitwall just beyond the timing line.

That freed up Verstappen to take a controlled victory (after a safety car period) in which he steadily built his lead over Lewis Hamilton and managed it easily until the end.

Hamilton’s second place was earned from a lightning start that vaulted him ahead of both McLarens and his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

And he was clearly the faster Ferrari in these conditions as Leclerc faded extremely badly late on, putting him under pressure from Oscar Piastri, Lando Norris and a muted championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Leclerc looked to have done enough to stave off the McLaren threat even before they collided calamitously on the final lap.

Norris launched a silly move on his team-mate into the Turn 5 right-hander. Piastri left some room on the inside but Norris, who went over the kerb, hit his team-mate's car and spun both of them round.

Though Norris rejoined after a short delay and claimed a point in eighth - a point he may lose given the incident is under investigation - Piastri retired in the wall.

This gifted Antonelli fourth and elevated several midfield cars into healthy points positions.

Liam Lawson spearheaded this group with a very accomplished drive to fifth while Ollie Bearman was sixth for Haas - keeping Nico Hulkenberg from his team’s championship rival Audi at bay in the process.

Hulkenberg had robustly passed Pierre Gasly earlier in the race to run behind Bearman but looked set to end the sprint empty-handed before McLaren imploded.

Among the nine retirees were also Isack Hadjar and Franco Colapinto, who suffered stoppages during the early safety car period, first-lap colliders Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez, and Alex Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas.

Albon and Bortoleto collided ahead of the safety car period ending in an incident that will be investigated after the race.

title: 'I just had nothing to lose' – Tiffany Cromwell delivers feisty farewell in Nannup at home UCI Gravel World Championships
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
The Australian rider has won at the SEVEN Gravel World Series race held in the same location three times, and she was going to make the most of that home advantage to time her moves.

"When you know it's your last one, the head space was good. I knew I just had nothing to lose," Cromwell told after crossing her final finish line.

The outcome was eighth as she took on her fifth and final Gravel Worlds, but she carved out a spectacular path along the way. The first key selection, as expected, was made on Brockman and Cromwell became part of the chase group, which through the next section just kept chipping away at the gap. Cromwell finally closed the last bit and rather than sitting in, decided she may as well just keep on going.

"In gravel, I've always been good at just getting in my rhythm, and I think just the dynamic at the front – nobody really wants to show their cards too quickly – it seemed to play into my favour."

Initially it looked like Cromwell's move would be short-lived, with Marianne Vos (Netherlands) among those to go out in pursuit, but then her rivals started looking at each other and the gap stretched, sitting at over a minute at 70km to go in the 125.6km race with 3,179m of elevation gain.

"It was obviously early on but It was like 'OK, you know, why not try something, get a head start," she said, who knew that she "always suffered" on the Ellis climb ahead.

"Getting that far and having the head start was perfect because then it put me really back in the game.

"I knew I couldn't match the girls on the climb, so I just had to take a chance, and I think it was just one of those days, you're just not thinking, you're not doubting yourself."

So even though she was caught, dropped and then clawed her way back again once more it was Cromwell who was charging into the brutal climb of Folly with just under 30km to go, delivering an excited roar and chatter from among the waiting crowd who hadn't been expecting her to be on the charge, or perhaps even in the lead group, once again.

"I was like, 'I'm cooked, I could sit here, get dropped in a few k or attack," she said. "And the way gravel works, a lot of individual riders against each other, nobody wants to necessarily chase straight away, so again, it just gave me another head start for Folly. But then I was like, done, done."

Though she still held on for a finish within the top ten, even sprinting to the line against Elisa Serné (Netherlands) to make sure she got eight and not ninth.

"I wanted to come here, race my bike, give everything I had, and just be at the finish having no regrets," concluded Cromwell as she did her final round of post-race media interviews to conclude a career spanning 17 seasons, and with a bank of many successes – which now includes her second UCI Gravel World Championships top 10.

title: Marianne Vos Wins UCI Gravel Worlds, Gomez Villafañe Sixth, Heavy Crash Mars Race
author: ahood
text:
Vos, pictured here in the 2024 edition, won her second UCI gravel worlds title in a wild race Saturday. (Photo: JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga via AFP)

Marianne Vos claimed a second UCI Gravel World Championship title Saturday in Nannup, Australia, winning solo after a showdown with Rosa Klöser as U.S.-based gravel star Sofia Gomez Villafañe finished sixth.

A heavy crash involving Geerike Schreurs and Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio overshadowed the race.

“This victory really means a lot to me,” Vos said.

Germany’s Klöser finished 27 seconds behind Vos after slipping out in the closing kilometers. Larissa Hartog took bronze for the Netherlands.

Gomez Villafañe, representing Argentina, crossed the line sixth at 5:15 back. Tiffany Cromwell, racing in her final pro race , attacked early before finishing eighth.

Vos and Klöser pulled clear late in the race to chase the rainbow jersey.

Vos, 39, accelerated inside the final four kilometers, and Klöser fought back onto her wheel before sliding out. The Dutchwoman soloed to the line to win her career 15th world title across different disciplines.

“There was more mud than I expected. As a result, there were also some slippery sections on the course, so we had to be careful at times. Rosa was incredibly strong, especially on the climbs, where I really had to dig deep to stay with her,” Vos said.

Nannup’s punishing 125.6km course with about 3,180m of climbing is the first gravel worlds held outside Europe .

The race started after a controversial late-hour UCI decision over points that impacted dozens of riders .

Cromwell gave the locals something to cheer about when she attacked early. The favorites organized a chase behind as Cromwell opened up a gap of 1:30.

Schreurs was involved in a heavy crash with about 70km to go.

The Dutch woman lost control while riding near the front of the chasing group, went off the gravel road, and hit the ground hard.

"She has not moved." "She’s badly hit her head." 🇿🇦 Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio and 🇳🇱 Geerike Schreurs suffered heavy falls in the elite women’s race, with red flags raised following the incidents. #NannupGravel2026 | October 10-11 | SBS & SBS On Demand 📺 pic.twitter.com/mXPa1JhJBT

Moolman-Pasio, also racing her final pro race , also crashed and remained nearby as medical staff attended to the Dutch rider. There was no immediate update on possible injuries.

Vos and Klöser caught Cromwell with about 24km to go and opened up a winning gap coming into the final 10km. Klöser slipped out on a corner, and Vos drove home the victory in a wild finale.

“It was a fantastic course here in Australia. I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here,” she said.

Vos now owns 15 elite world titles across four disciplines: eight in cyclocross, three on the road, two on the track and, with her win in Australia, two in gravel.

title: Telegraph owner poised to make newsroom job cuts in investment promise U-turn
author: Michael Savage Media editor
text:
Exclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundancies

The new owner of the Telegraph is preparing to make significant job cuts to its newsroom, just months after stating it would invest in the title to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.

Axel Springer, the German media company overseen by its billionaire chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to be examining proposals that would make between 50 and 100 journalists redundant.

A source familiar with the plans said a forthcoming consultation was likely to propose cutting a “significant proportion” of editorial staff, possibly before Christmas.

They said such proposals called into question Axel Springer’s promise to “back an investment programme in [the Telegraph Media Group] to grow and expand the business”.

A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group declined to comment. No redundancies have been announced to staff so far.

It would mark the first big intervention by Axel Springer since its £575m purchase of the Telegraph earlier this year. The sale ended three tortuous years for the Telegraph and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.

The proposed cuts have confused some Telegraph figures, who are struggling to understand how it aligns with Döpfner’s pledge to “bring that uncertainty to an end”.

At a recent Axel Springer leadership summit held in London, Döpfner is also said to have stated that the company could not cut its way to growth.

Axel Springer, which also owns Politico and the German titles Bild and Die Welt, recently brought in consultants to examine the financial health of the Telegraph titles, which include the Daily Telegraph, the Sunday Telegraph and its online news operation.

Döpfner has made no secret of his desire to boost the Telegraph’s US operation , with senior editors already deployed to the US to develop those plans.

However, consultants are understood to have drawn up potential cuts to the existing news operation at the 171-year-old titles.

Sources said consultants had also recommended that the Telegraph set up side projects to support its journalism, such as price comparison sites and healthcare. Some insiders were said to be baffled by some of the suggestions.

A source familiar with the proposals said they would anger Telegraph staff, who had hoped Axel Springer’s ownership would mark the arrival of “sunny uplands” after three years of being “starved of any form of investment, pay rises or management changes that could move us on”.

“The path to growth is not to cut jobs,” they said. “They’re still going to need to hire people in the States if they’re going to make any sort of push there, but staff haven’t been told where that money is going to come from.”

The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed that it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m.

However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.

title: Sprint start crash causes huge tension within Aprilia
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
Raul Fernandez has repeatedly excoriated Aprilia stablemate Marco Bezzecchi for his role in setting up their crash at the start of the Mandalika sprint, describing Bezzecchi's tactics as "not nice", "ungentlemanly" and "not clever".

Fernandez fractured his left index finger in the crash at the start of the sprint, which was triggered as four riders - Fernandez, Bezzecchi, Marc Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio - went into Turn 1 almost side-by-side and their lines converged deep into the corner.

As Di Giannantonio ran Marquez out wide, Bezzecchi checked up and had contact with Fernandez that took both out of the race and injured the latter. Fernandez is now in doubt for the grand prix, but will try to contest the warm-up.

Fernandez was seething after the sprint, giving explosive interviews to both Spanish broadcaster DAZN and Italian broadcaster Sky Sport, in which he effectively accused Bezzecchi of deliberately compromising his race at the cost of letting two Ducatis through.

His tone softened between the TV interviews and the written media, but his argument remained the same. Bezzecchi, he felt, approached Turn 1 with the focus only on beating Fernandez, squeezed him out and left the door open for the two Ducatis, which created the conditions for the crash.

"For me, the crash is a consequence of the start," Fernandez said. "On the start, for me I tried to keep my bike in the middle of the track, to try to not open the door for other riders to overtake. Marco had made a really good start and he overtook me - he didn't really overtake 100 percent, but he put the bike close to me and started to take me out the track.

"And this is for me the more frustrating thing about today. When you want to do something that is not clean in this sport. We are riders, we put our body [on the line] at more than 300km/h and when you are doing something that you know that is not really nice, I am not happy with that.

"And for me the version is, OK, we crash, it doesn't matter, it can happen, one day it will be me that I will make a mistake, another day will be another rider. The problem is when you are making something that you know is not nice. And for me this is the big problem that we saw today.

"We go out [wide] he doesn't give me space, two Ducatis overtook us, we crash, that's it."

Fernandez chuckled that it was "for sure not good" as a strategy by Bezzecchi. He said the Aprilia riders knew the battle for victory would play out between them, and accused Bezzecchi of "thinking just of me".

"I am not playing for the championship. He was playing for the championship. For me he was not very smart."

He also indicated he was more upset with Bezzecchi over this than with Jorge Martin over the Balaton Park pile-up at Turn 1, as that had been a mere mistake and this was a premeditated "bad action to another rider".

He said it was nothing that could or should be penalised but that Bezzecchi "didn't have the respect" and that, while Aprilia riders are told to be "gentlemen" with one another in terms of wheel-to-wheel racing, it "looks like he [Bezzecchi] was not a gentleman with us".

Bezzecchi defends himself

Bezzecchi was told of Fernandez's incandescence but chalked it up to heat-of-the-moment emotions clouding Fernandez's judgment. "I am maybe the one who can confirm this more than anyone," he joked, in seeming reference to his ban at Assen for striking a marshal.

It was a "racing incident", Bezzecchi insisted. "I was just looking to put myself in the best place possible for the braking. I knew Marc could try to overtake but was for me useless to try to force too much and maybe throw away the race in the first corner.

"It's what I did. If Raul is angry, I'm sorry, but honestly, he touched me! So at the end there's nothing to be angry for. Me versus him or him versus me, at the end it was a racing incident. I couldn't disappear and he also couldn't disappear. I don't want to waste energy with this, I want to focus for tomorrow."

How the Ducati pair saw it

Marquez, who went on to win the sprint, said the incident was "easy to explain".

"Four bikes in parallel, and I believe that Bezzecchi was looking at Raul, to brake a bit later, I was looking at Bezzecchi to brake a bit later, and Diggia was looking at me to brake a bit later. The consequence - four riders out of the line and [Jorge] Martin from fifth to first," he recounted.

Di Giannantonio had been completely unaware that anyone had crashed - but did say that contact with Marquez coming through the corner caused a downshift on his end that then compromised his exit from Turn 1.

"Honestly, you have to ask the others [about the incident] - me, I just got hit again."

title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
author: Robert Tait in Washington, and Oliver Holmes
text:
President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies

Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.

Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.

In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.

“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”

He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”

Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.

Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.

“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”

Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.

“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X . “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”

Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.

“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.

“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.

Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”

But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
text:
George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field

The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.

The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.

The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.

“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.

In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.

“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.

Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”

He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.

Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation , and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030 .

“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.

“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK .”

Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”

Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.

Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.

In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology.

Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”

“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.

“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.

Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”

He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”

Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards .

“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

title: 'At the end of the day, you can only try' – Despite puncture and a late crash, Rosa Klöser claws back silver at UCI Gravel World Championships
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
It was just 20km into the UCI Gravel World Championships elite women's race on Saturday and Rosa Klöser (Germany) thought it may have already been over, when a tricky flat dropped her out of the lead group not long before the first crucial climb of the day.

But somehow, some 100km later, she was out front with Marianne Vos (Netherlands) and contending for the win.

"It was definitely a tough race. I mean, the course is really relentless," Klöser told after going to the podium to claim her silver medal.

The bad luck also seemed to be just as relentless for the rider wearing the number 13 on her back, as it turned out her flat tyre wouldn't be the only misfortune of her day.

"It was a really big job for me to come back because it was also not easy to find the hole in my tyre, so it took me really quite a while until I got going again," said Klöser. "And if I'm honest, I saw the race move away from me there, but I was like, 'OK, you know what, you can only try'. So I kept pushing, and when I could see them I got an extra gear and I managed to come back to the front group,"

The front group ebbed and flowed as groups rejoined and then were again shed on the unrelenting course and a caught stick caused another quick stop for Klöser , that, however was quickly dealt with and the Canyon-SRAM-MAAP rider went with Vos at around 20km to go

Once she made it, however, her travails weren't over, with a stick caught in her rear mech, but that barely made a dent compared to the other chase back which could well have weakened her sprint.

Klöser, who has also spent a considerable amount of time on the road this year, jumped back into gravel with a couple of UCI Gravel World Series races in September, winning both and in one of them, Sea Otter Europe, shaking off Vos. It's clear that Klöser was coming into the race with a course that seemed to suit her and some powerful form.

"I won't lie, it was a really big goal," said Kloser, who did have her season interrupted by a parasitic infection that she was unaware of, but worked it out in time to prepare for the rainbow jersey race.

As the final 10km approached, it looked set to come down to a sprint battle between Vos, who is renowned for her prowess in delivering a sprint finish at the end of a tough race, and Klöser, who managed to pull off a huge gravel win when she clinched Unbound in a sprint of nine. But more bad luck struck before Klöser could even think about the sprint.

"Unfortunately, I think with 4km to go, I wiped out in like the last technical corner," said the rider who fronted up for the podium ceremonies and post-race interviews with a ripped shorts, a wound on one leg and a banged-up arm.

"I probably overinflated my tyre also a bit when when it got flat. But I mean that's racing, that's gravel. At the end of the day, you can only try."

title: Why Martin had to give up MotoGP sprint win
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
MotoGP's former championship leader Jorge Martin had to surrender the Mandalika sprint win and points lead due to the risk of a tyre pressure infringement.

After an opening-corner melee removed fellow Aprilia riders Raul Fernandez and Marco Bezzecchi from the picture, and gave Martin 'free' passage into first from fifth on the grid, the Aprilia man looked to be in control and en route to a comfortable victory.

But Martin suddenly slowed and allowed title rival Marc Marquez through, in a move that looked like a bid to get some heat onto his front tyre and avoid a ruinous eight-second penalty for non-compliance.

The front tyre must be kept above the baseline pressure - around 1.8 bar, though it varies slightly from round to round - for at least 30% of the total laps in the sprint - and Martin confirmed after the race that this was indeed the reason why he had to abandon the lead.

His attempts to then strike back on Marquez came to naught, and a mistake on the penultimate lap dropped him to fourth place - turning what was set to be a five-point lead over Marquez exiting the race into a four-point deficit.

"I didn't do a great start but they were four[-wide] into first corner so it was easy for me to go into the lead," Martin recounted. "Then I tried to push and I was able to make a big gap to Marc. But then I realised that I was under the pressure [requirement]. I tried to push the front more, tried to warm it a bit more, but it wasn't into the [legal] zone.

"So I had to let Marc past, and then after that everything started to get a bit difficult. Even if I was trying to be close [to Marquez] to make a move into the last lap - that's why I made a mistake with two laps to go, and then the chances were gone."

Martin felt that he still carried a "big opportunity" into Sunday to re-assert himself in the championship race.

"For sure tomorrow Marco [Bezzecchi] and [Raul] Fernandez will be super strong - but so will I," he said, albeit perhaps unaware that Fernandez is believed to have sustained a hand injury in the Turn 1 crash.

Why was the pressure too low?

Martin and his crew chief Daniele Romagnoli may not have expected to lead the race - given he was fifth on the grid, and didn't necessarily have the pace to easily clear his fellow Aprilias.

But Martin insisted they didn't set the front tyre pressure particularly low in the expectation of running in the pack.

"It's not a thing that we normally do. We never risk with the tyre pressure, I don't know why today we were out [of the limit].

"I think here it's quite difficult with the humidity, and maybe it changed from yesterday. But honestly we didn't risk.

"Sometimes it happens. It hasn't happened to me a lot in the last few years, but today [it has]. So for sure it's something we need to check, because it's something that today maybe 0.1 [bar higher] I was able to win the same and not be in trouble."

title: 'We cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying' –Riders stage remarkable protest at Il Lombardia as Evenepoel delivers speech on safety
author: Matilda Price
text:
There were remarkable scenes at the start of Il Lombardia on Saturday morning, as the peloton staged a protest and refused to start the race for a full five minutes.

Even more remarkably, Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) grabbed a microphone and delivered a speech, explaining to the race organisers and the general public that the riders were making a statement over rider safety.

Suspicions that some sort of protest might be brewing were raised when Evenepoel, Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5) and Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) approached the senior race officials on the start line, a few minutes prior to the start of the race.

It would appear there was no more forewarning than that, as the race’s official master of ceremonies began the countdown from 10 seconds to the race start, only for the riders to remain unmoved when the start of the race was signalled.

After around two minutes, in which the race speaker declared "some sort of delay", Evenepoel was handed a microphone and addressed the gathered public in the centre of Bergamo.

"I will speak in English in the name of the whole bunch and not only the guys who are here but everyone in pro cycling," he said.

"We want to make this statement because there's too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race. Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do," he said, making reference to the death of Finlay Tarling.

"So this is why we want to spend five minutes more still to make our statement towards organisations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling, because we cannot accept the fact that people are dying. This is why we stand still, we pay our tribute and respect to all the riders who are already involved in incidents.

"To the organisers who organise races in the future, please make sure that we can race safely, and that we can just do what we like to do without being worried about cars, motorbikes, all that stuff, coming into the course."

Evenepoel's speech was met with applause from the spectators and his fellow riders.

'We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act'

Tom Pidcock , whose teammates were involved in the incident at Tre Valli Varesine – and admitted he nearly stopped riding then – has been vocal about the issue of safety, and posted a statement to his Instagram to coincide with the protest. Various other riders posted the same joint statement.

"As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to," it read.

"This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

"This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer. Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

"We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

"After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one. We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones."

CPA president Adam Hansen shared the same statement on his Twitter account on Saturday morning.

After around five minutes of standstill, the flag was dropped for a second time and the peloton rolled out for the neutralised start.

RCS, who organise Il Lombardia but not any of the earlier Italian races where incidents have occurred, voiced their support for the protest, though without mentioning the demand for race organisers to act.

"At the start of Il Lombardia presented by Crédit Agricole, the riders came together to send an important message, stopping for five minutes to urge all road users to behave responsibly and show mutual respect, both during races and in everyday life," a release from the organisers read. "RCS Sport fully supports this appeal, aimed at ensuring everyone's safety."
